title: 01-01-00 Introduction to Computational Statistics and Data-Driven Thinking
content: In 1946, mathematician Stanislaw Ulam was recovering from a serious illness and passing the hours playing solitaire. Halfway through a game, he wondered: what is the exact probability that a well-shuffled deck of Canfield solitaire comes out completely solvable? He tried attacking it with classical combinatorics—counting permutations, tracking blocked cards—and quickly realized the algebra was a hopeless tangle. Then a thought struck him: why not simply deal 100 hands, count how many win, and let a fast electronic computer deal 100,000 hands in seconds? Together with John von Neumann, Ulam turned that bedside insight into the Monte Carlo method —the birth of modern computational statistics. The goal of this opening lesson is not to hand you a stack of formulas to memorize. It is to shift how you think about randomness: away from “can I solve this integral on paper?” and toward “can I simulate this system honestly on a computer and measure how accurate my simulation is?” By the end, you will contrast classical analytic statistics with computational statistics, calculate Monte Carlo uncertainty by hand, and see the Law of Large Numbers turn raw repetition into rigorous statistical knowledge. --- Key ideas: What Fields Sit Behind Computational Statistics? Before diving into code, it helps to see the three pillars of probability and statistics that make computational thinking work. 1. Probability Theory and Limit Theorems Probability theory models random experiments using random variables, distributions, expectations MATH , and variances MATH . Two cornerstone theorems bridge single random draws and reliable long-run behavior: the Law of Large Numbers LLN sample averages converge to the true mean and the Central Limit Theorem CLT sample averages fluctuate around the true mean like a bell curve of width MATH . - Core questions: How fast does an empirical average approach the true expectation? How many trials MATH do we need to guarantee a given margin of error? - Real-world reach: Insurance pricing, reliability engineering, clinical-trial sample-size planning, and polling accuracy. 2. Computational Statistics and Resampling Monte Carlo & Bootstrap When real-world models involve correlated portfolios, non-normal tails, or complex nonlinear rules, closed-form formulas vanish. Computational statistics replaces paper-and-pencil derivations with algorithmic simulation: Monte Carlo simulates from a known probabilistic model, while the Bootstrap resamples directly from observed data to estimate uncertainty without assuming a textbook bell curve. - Core questions: How do we estimate intractable probabilities, integrals, and confidence intervals using random sampling? How can we reduce simulation variance? - Real-world reach: Financial risk modeling Value-at-Risk , Bayesian MCMC inference, A/B testing with skewed revenue metrics, and physics particle transport. 3. Statistical Inference and Data-Driven Modeling Statistical inference flips probability backwards: instead of knowing the mechanism and predicting the data, we observe finite noisy data and infer the unknown mechanism behind it—quantifying our uncertainty honestly rather than pretending a point estimate is exact. - Core questions: Given a finite sample, what range of parameter values is plausible? How do we separate genuine signal from sampling noise? - Real-world reach: Medical diagnostics, econometric forecasting, quality control, and machine-learning evaluation. --- Why computational statistics? Suppose you want the probability that the sum of ten fair dice exceeds 40. A classical solution uses combinatorics or a normal approximation the Central Limit Theorem . That can be elegant when the math cooperates. Change the problem slightly—say, the probability of a large joint loss in a portfolio of 50 correlated stocks with heavy-tailed jumps—and a closed-form expression is usually out of reach. Computational statistics is what you do then. Instead of hunting for a perfect equation that describes the world, you imitate the world: generate synthetic copies of the experiment, repeat them thousands or millions of times, and count. Abstract probability becomes a concrete programming problem, and many questions that defeat analytic methods become transparent. Analytic versus computational statistics | Aspect | Classical Analytic Statistics | Computational Statistics | |--------|----------------------------------|--------------------------| | Core engine | Closed-form theorems & parametric assumptions | Repeated random simulation & resampling | | Classic CI for a mean | MATH relies on normality/CLT | Bootstrap empirical percentiles from resampled data | | Strength | Exact, instantaneous, reveals algebraic scaling laws | Handles messy, correlated, non-normal models easily | | Main cost | Breaks down when assumptions fail | CPU time & Monte Carlo error of order MATH | Neither replaces the other: great statisticians use analytic theory to understand how an estimator scales and computational methods to evaluate it when exact formulas do not exist. Simulation and the law of large numbers The engine is Monte Carlo simulation . If you want to know an unknown probability MATH , define an indicator random variable MATH if event MATH happens on trial MATH and MATH otherwise. After MATH independent trials, your estimate is simply the empirical frequency MATH . What makes this mathematically legitimate is the Law of Large Numbers . As the number of trials MATH grows, the sample mean converges in probability to the true expectation: MATH On a computer, MATH is simply the number of loop iterations you can afford—and crucially, the standard error of your Monte Carlo estimate shrinks as MATH --- Worked Example 1: The Birthday Problem by Hand vs. Monte Carlo Uncertainty In a room of MATH people ignoring leap years , what is the probability that at least two share a birthday? title: 01-02-00 Overview of Supervised Learning
content: Imagine two students preparing for a final exam using a past practice test. Student A refuses to study any formulas and simply guesses the average answer for every question—scoring poorly on both the practice test and the real exam. Student B memorizes every single answer key from the practice test word-for-word, scoring a flawless 100% on the practice sheet—and then bombs the real exam the moment the numbers change slightly. Those two students are the living faces of underfitting high bias and overfitting high variance . Supervised learning is the art of learning from labeled past examples MATH so that your predictions hold up on brand-new, unseen data. This lesson builds the statistical-learning frame, separates regression from classification, derives the bias–variance decomposition with a concrete hand calculation, and shows why high-dimensional feature spaces quietly ambush naive models through the curse of dimensionality . --- Key ideas: What Fields Sit Behind Supervised Learning? Supervised learning is not merely software engineering—it rests on three mathematical pillars. 1. Statistical Decision Theory Loss & Risk Given random inputs MATH and target MATH drawn from an unknown joint distribution MATH , decision theory defines a loss function MATH measuring the cost of a wrong prediction and seeks the predictor MATH that minimizes expected risk MATH . Under squared error, the theoretical ideal predictor is the conditional expectation MATH . - Core questions: Which loss function matches the real cost of errors L2 vs. L1 vs. cross-entropy ? What is the theoretically lowest achievable error Bayes risk ? - Real-world reach: Credit scoring, demand forecasting, spam filtering, and medical triage models. 2. Estimation Theory and the Bias–Variance Tradeoff Because we never know the true distribution MATH , we estimate MATH from a finite noisy training sample of size MATH . Estimation theory decomposes expected squared prediction error into Bias² systematic misspecification , Variance sensitivity to which training sample we happened to draw , and Irreducible Noise MATH . - Core questions: How does adding parameters trade lower bias for higher variance? How do regularization and ensembles rebalance that trade? - Real-world reach: Choosing model complexity, Ridge/Lasso shrinkage, Random Forests variance reduction , and Gradient Boosting bias reduction . 3. High-Dimensional Geometry The Curse of Dimensionality In 1D or 2D, nearby training points sit close together so local averaging works effortlessly. As the number of features MATH climbs to 50 or 500, high-dimensional geometry behaves counterintuitively: almost all volume migrates to the outer boundary shell, and pairwise distances concentrate so that “nearest” neighbors are barely closer than average points. - Core questions: How many samples MATH are needed to cover a MATH -dimensional space? Why do we need structural assumptions linearity, sparsity, manifolds in high dimensions? - Real-world reach: Genomics MATH , recommendation systems, image/text embeddings, and dimensionality reduction PCA . --- What is supervised learning? A training set consists of labeled pairs MATH : - MATH : the feature predictor vector - MATH : the target response Goal: learn a function MATH from training data such that MATH on unseen future draws of MATH . Two main problem types 1. Regression: MATH is continuous Examples: house prices, temperature, sales. 2. Classification: MATH is categorical Examples: spam / not spam, handwritten digits, disease diagnosis. python import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.datasets import make regression, make classification from sklearn.model selection import train test split def visualize supervised learning : """Contrast a regression cloud with a two-class classification cloud.""" fig, axes = plt.subplots 1, 2, figsize= 14, 5 X reg, y reg = make regression n samples=100, n features=1, noise=10, random state=42 axes 0 .scatter X reg, y reg, alpha=0.6, s=50 axes 0 .set xlabel 'Feature X' axes 0 .set ylabel 'Target Y continuous ' axes 0 .set title 'Regression: predict a continuous value' axes 0 .grid True, alpha=0.3 X clf, y clf = make classification n samples=200, n features=2, n redundant=0, n informative=2, n clusters per class=1, random state=42 colors = 'red' if label == 0 else 'blue' for label in y clf axes 1 .scatter X clf :, 0 , X clf :, 1 , c=colors, alpha=0.6, s=50 axes 1 .set xlabel 'Feature X₁' axes 1 .set ylabel 'Feature X₂' axes 1 .set title 'Classification: binary labels' axes 1 .grid True, alpha=0.3 plt.tight layout plt.show visualize supervised learning Loss functions and training error A loss MATH scores the discrepancy between the truth MATH and the prediction MATH . Common losses Regression: - Squared error L2 : MATH — heavily penalizes large errors; minimized by the conditional mean . - Absolute error L1 : MATH — robust to outliers; minimized by the conditional median . Classification: - 0–1 loss: MATH — counts misclassifications directly, but non-differentiable. - Cross-entropy: MATH — smooth, convex surrogate that rewards well-calibrated probabilities. Training error empirical risk : MATH This is error on data the model has already seen. Test error expected prediction error : MATH This is the error we actually care about: performance on fresh draws from the population. The central tension: training error keeps falling as the model gets more flexible; test error forms a U-shape and rebounds upward once the model starts memorizing noise. That rebound is overfitting . python from sklearn.linear model import LinearRegression from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures from sklearn.metrics import mean squared error def plt.plot degrees, train errors, 'o-', label='Training error', linewidth=2 plt.plot degrees, test errors, 's-', label='Test error', linewidth=2 plt.xlabel 'Model complexity polynomial degree ' data, four different degrees' plt.legend plt.grid True, alpha=0.3 plt.tight layout plt.show optimal degree = degrees np.argmin test errors print f"Degree with smallest test error: optimal degree " print f"Minimum test error: min test errors :.4f " demonstrate overfitting The bias–variance tradeoff Suppose MATH where MATH and MATH . For any estimator MATH trained on a random training set, its expected squared test error at a fixed point MATH splits exactly into three pieces: MATH 1. Bias. Error from a model that is too rigid to represent the true relationship. High bias is underfitting fitting a straight line to a sine wave . 2. Variance. Error from a model that chases random fluctuations in the particular training sample. High variance is overfitting a degree-15 polynomial wiggling wildly through 14 points . 3. Irreducible error MATH . Inherent randomness in MATH that no model can ever predict away. --- Worked Example 1: Exact Bias–Variance–Noise Accounting by Hand Let’s make the decomposition completely concrete with zero simulation required. Shrunk estimator: MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | Look at row D! By deliberately introducing a tiny bit of bias MATH via shrinkage toward a reasonable prior guess, we slashed variance from MATH down to MATH —beating the unbiased sample mean MATH ! That single 4-row table is the entire mathematical justification for Ridge regression and regularization . --- python def bias variance decomposition n simulations=100 : """Resample training sets and watch bias shrink while variance grows.""" def true function x : return np.sin 2 np.pi x x test = np.array 0.5 y true = true function x test degrees = 1, 3, 9, 15 results = deg: 'predictions': , 'bias': 0, 'variance': 0 for deg in degrees for in range n simulations : X train = np.random.uniform 0, 1, 20 .reshape -1, 1 y train = true function X train .ravel + np.random.normal 0, 0.2, 20 for degree in degrees: poly = PolynomialFeatures degree=degree X train poly = poly.fit transform X train x test poly = poly.transform x test.reshape -1, 1 model = LinearRegression model.fit X train poly, y train results degree 'predictions' .append model.predict x test poly 0 for degree in degrees: preds = np.array results degree 'predictions' mean pred = preds.mean results degree 'bias' = mean pred - y true 0 2 results degree 'variance' = preds.var results degree 'mse' = results degree 'bias' + results degree 'variance' fig, axes = plt.subplots 1, 2, figsize= 14, 5 axes 0 .axhline y true 0 , color='green', linestyle='--', linewidth=2, label='True value' for degree in degrees: axes 0 .hist results degree 'predictions' , bins=20, alpha=0.5, label=f'Degree degree ' axes 0 .set xlabel 'Predicted value at x = 0.5' axes 0 .set ylabel 'Frequency' axes 0 .set title 'Prediction distribution across training sets' axes 0 .legend axes 0 .grid True, alpha=0.3 x pos = np.arange len degrees bias vals = results d 'bias' for d in degrees var vals = results d 'variance' for d in degrees axes 1 .bar x pos - Sample size. Matching a given density in MATH dimensions needs on the order of MATH points. 2. Distances fade. In high dimensions, almost every point sits near the outer shell, and nearest neighbors are nearly as far as distant points. 3. Overfitting becomes effortless. With more feature axes, a flexible model can easily align with pure noise. --- Worked Example 2: The Curse of Dimensionality in Two Back-of-the-Envelope Calculations Imagine points drawn uniformly inside the MATH -dimensional unit hypercube MATH . 1. title: 00-01-01 Continuity and Uniform Continuity
content: Imagine training a statistical model by nudging its parameters slightly—say moving a weight by MATH —and watching the loss suddenly skyrocket by MATH . On paper, the loss function might be completely “continuous,” with no jumps or breaks anywhere. Yet numerically, your optimizer explodes! Why? Because ordinary continuity only promises that small input nudges keep output changes small near one fixed point —it makes no promise that the same step size works safely across the entire domain. This short mathematical reference builds the three-level ladder of smoothness— continuity , uniform continuity , and Lipschitz continuity —that quietly controls whether gradient descent converges, whether probability densities behave cleanly, and why bounded domains save numerical algorithms from blowing up. --- Key ideas: Why Do Continuity Notions Matter in Statistics & ML? Real analysis can feel abstract until you see where each definition shows up in statistical algorithms. 1. Real Analysis and MATH – MATH Precision Real analysis replaces hand-waving “draw it without lifting your pencil” with exact quantifier logic: for every target tolerance MATH , how small must the input perturbation MATH be? Swapping the order of just two quantifiers turns pointwise continuity into uniform continuity. - Core questions: Does a single step size MATH work everywhere on the domain? Does a continuous function attain a global minimum on a closed bounded set Weierstrass Extreme Value Theorem ? - Real-world reach: Guaranteeing that maximum likelihood estimators exist and that numerical integration converges. 2. Optimization Theory and Lipschitz Smoothness When you train logistic regression, ridge regression, or a neural network with gradient descent MATH , how large can you safely set the learning rate MATH ? Lipschitz continuity gives the exact answer: if the loss or its gradient has Lipschitz constant MATH , you get a concrete global speed limit on how fast values or slopes can change. - Core questions: How big can a step size MATH be without overshooting the valley? How fast does gradient descent converge? - Real-world reach: Tuning learning rates, gradient clipping in deep learning, and Wasserstein GANs which explicitly enforce 1-Lipschitz critics . 3. Stability and Robustness in Statistical Learning In statistics, data always carry measurement noise. If an estimator or prediction map is Lipschitz with a small constant MATH , small perturbations in the input data produce small, predictable changes in the output—the mathematical backbone of adversarial robustness and differential privacy . - Core questions: How sensitive is a model’s prediction to tiny input noise or one altered training point? - Real-world reach: Robust regression Huber loss , adversarial defense in computer vision, and privacy-preserving data release. --- Continuity and uniform continuity Continuity and uniform continuity describe how “predictable” a function is. title: 00-01-02 Derivatives and Multivariable Calculus
content: Stand blindfolded on a foggy mountain range and try to hike down to the lowest valley. You cannot see the whole landscape at once—all you can feel under your boots is the local tilt of the ground which way is steepest downhill and its local curvature whether you are in a round bowl, on a narrow ridge, or at a mountain pass . That blindfolded hike is literally how modern statistics and machine learning fit models: whether you are solving ordinary least squares, maximizing a log-likelihood, or training a billion-parameter neural network, you are navigating a high-dimensional loss surface using gradients , Hessians , and the chain rule . This reference turns multivariable calculus from a list of formulas into a working compass for statistical optimization—showing you how to compute gradients and Hessians by hand on real regression losses and why curvature separates slow zig-zagging from rapid convergence. --- Key ideas: Where Does Multivariable Calculus Power Statistics? Three pillars connect undergraduate calculus directly to statistical estimation and machine learning. 1. Differential Calculus & First-Order Optimization Gradients The gradient MATH generalizes the single-variable derivative MATH to functions of MATH parameters. It points in the exact direction of steepest ascent; moving in the opposite direction MATH is gradient descent , the workhorse algorithm of modern machine learning. - Core questions: Where does MATH critical points ? Which direction shrinks the loss fastest at the current parameter vector? - Real-world reach: Maximum likelihood estimation MLE , logistic regression, stochastic gradient descent SGD , and Adam optimizers. 2. Second-Order Geometry & Curvature The Hessian Matrix Setting MATH only tells you the ground is flat—you might be at a minimum, a maximum, or a treacherous saddle point . The Hessian matrix MATH captures local curvature in every direction. Its eigenvalues tell you whether the surface curves upward like a bowl convex minimum and how stretched or narrow the valley is condition number . - Core questions: Is a critical point a true local minimum? How does Newton–Raphson use MATH to jump straight to the bottom of a quadratic bowl? - Real-world reach: Fisher Information Matrix in statistical inference computing standard errors of MLEs! , Newton–Raphson / L-BFGS solvers, and diagnosing ill-conditioned regression features. 3. The multivariable chain rule propagates sensitivity cleanly through any number of layers, forming the exact mathematical engine behind backpropagation . - Core questions: How does nudging an early parameter affect the final loss several layers downstream? - Real-world reach: Deep learning frameworks PyTorch, JAX , sensitivity analysis, and delta-method variance propagation in statistics. --- Derivatives and rate of change For a function of one variable, the derivative is the instantaneous slope—the local linear story of how the function moves. title: 01-07-00 Cross-Validation and Resampling Methods
content: Suppose you have only 100 patient records—expensive, hard-won clinical data—and you want to pick the best regularization strength MATH for a predictive model. If you lock away 30% as a validation set, you shrink your training set to 70 patients, and your choice of MATH might swing wildly depending on which 30 patients happened to land in the hold-out split. Yet if you score models on the training set itself, the most complex overfitted model wins every time! Cross-validation and the bootstrap solve this dilemma through a remarkably clever idea: reuse the data you already have, systematically holding out different slices in rotation so every observation gets a turn as both teacher and exam question. This lesson builds MATH -fold CV, Leave-One-Out CV, Stratified CV, and the Bootstrap—complete with concrete hand calculations and honest guidance on when each method shines. --- Key ideas: What Statistical Ideas Power Resampling? Resampling looks like simple data-shuffling, yet three deep statistical principles govern why it works—and when it fails. 1. Out-of-Sample Generalization & Empirical Risk Training error systematically underestimates future test error because the model has already adapted to the noise in the training sample optimism bias . Resampling simulates fresh test draws internally by partitioning the observed sample into disjoint fit and evaluation blocks. - Core questions: How accurately does cross-validation estimate expected test error? How does fold size affect bias and variance of the error estimate? - Real-world reach: Hyperparameter tuning GridSearchCV , model comparison, and preventing overfitting across tabular, vision, and NLP workflows. 2. Exchangeability, Stratification, and Dependence Structure Standard MATH -fold CV assumes observations are exchangeable shuffling rows does not break the data-generating process . When classes are severely imbalanced e.g., 2% fraud , random folds create noisy class ratios—fixed by Stratified MATH -fold . When data are ordered in time stocks, weather or grouped by patient/user, random shuffling leaks future or subject-level information—requiring time-series or group splits . - Core questions: Which observations are truly independent? What structural boundaries must never be crossed between train and validation? - Real-world reach: Fraud detection, clinical multi-hospital studies, and financial time-series forecasting. 3. Nonparametric Resampling The Bootstrap Invented by Bradley Efron 1979 , the bootstrap treats the empirical sample as a miniature stand-in for the unknown population, drawing MATH observations with replacement MATH times. Beyond estimating out-of-bag prediction error, it computes standard errors and confidence intervals for almost any statistic medians, ratios, AUC without assuming normality. - Core questions: How much of the original sample is left “out-of-bag” in each bootstrap draw? When does the bootstrap accurately mimic the true sampling distribution? - Real-world reach: Random Forests bagging + out-of-bag error , A/B test confidence intervals for skewed metrics, and econometric standard errors. --- The problem: training error is the wrong score Training error is a poor proxy for real performance: - It falls monotonically as the model becomes more flexible. - Test error on unseen data is what we actually care about. Because we never have an infinite test set, we spend our finite training sample carefully to estimate test error. python import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.model selection import train test split, cross val score, KFold from sklearn.linear model import Ridge from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures from sklearn.pipeline import make pipeline from sklearn.datasets import make regression def demonstrate train test split : """A single 70/30 split already shows the U-shaped test-error curve.""" np.random.seed 42 X, y = make regression n samples=100, n features=1, noise=10 X train, X test, y train, y test = train test split X, y, test size=0.3, random state=42 degrees = range 1, 16 train errors = test errors = for degree in degrees: model = make pipeline PolynomialFeatures degree , Ridge alpha=0.1 model.fit X train, y train train errors.append np.mean y train - model.predict X train 2 test errors.append np.mean y test - model.predict X test 2 plt.figure figsize= 10, 6 plt.plot degrees, train errors, 'o-', label='Training error', linewidth=2 plt.plot degrees, test errors, 's-', label='Test error', linewidth=2 plt.xlabel 'Polynomial degree' plt.ylabel 'Mean squared error' plt.title 'Training vs test error' plt.legend plt.grid True, alpha=0.3 plt.show optimal degree = degrees np.argmin test errors print f"Optimal degree: optimal degree " print f"Test error at that degree: min test errors :.4f " demonstrate train test split MATH -fold cross-validation Instead of betting everything on one random split, cut the data into MATH disjoint folds commonly MATH or MATH : 1. Partition the sample into MATH pieces of nearly equal size. 2. For each MATH : - hold fold MATH out as validation, - train on the remaining MATH folds, - record the validation error MATH . 3. Average across all MATH folds: MATH Why it helps: every single observation is evaluated out-of-sample exactly once, reducing the random luck of a single train/validation cut. --- Worked Example 1: Computing LOOCV by Hand on a 3-Point Dataset Let’s run Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation MATH completely by hand on three observations MATH using the simplest possible model: predict the training sample mean MATH . | Fold | Held-out point MATH | Training set | Training prediction MATH | Squared error MATH | |------|------------------------|--------------|----------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------| | 1 | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | | 2 | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | | 3 | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | - Training MSE fitting MATH to all 3 points : MATH . - LOOCV MSE: MATH ! Notice two illuminating facts: 1 Training MSE MATH is less than half of the honest out-of-sample LOOCV error MATH ; and 2 for any linear smoother, LOOCV satisfies an exact shortcut formula MATH here MATH , so MATH —letting you compute LOOCV for ordinary least squares in one fit! . --- python def k fold cross validation demo : """Compare 5-fold CV with one holdout when choosing Ridge's α.""" np.random.seed 42 X, y = make regression n samples=100, n features=5, noise=10 alphas = np.logspace -2, 3, 20 kf = KFold n splits=5, shuffle=True, random state=42 cv scores = for alpha in alphas: model = Ridge alpha=alpha scores = cross val score model, X, y, cv=kf, scoring='neg mean squared error' cv scores.append -scores.mean X train, X test, y train, y test = train test split X, y, test size=0.2, random state=42 single split scores = for alpha in alphas: model = Ridge alpha=alpha model.fit X train, y train pred = model.predict X test single split scores.append np.mean y test - pred 2 plt.figure figsize= 10, 6 plt.semilogx alphas, cv scores, 'o-', label='5-fold CV', linewidth=2, markersize=6 plt.semilogx alphas, single split scores, 's--', label='Single train/test split', linewidth=2, markersize=6, alpha=0.7 plt.xlabel 'Regularization parameter α ' plt.ylabel 'Mean squared error' plt.title 'K-fold CV vs a single split' plt.legend plt.grid True, alpha=0.3 plt.show print f"Optimal α CV : alphas np.argmin cv scores :.4f " print f"Optimal α single split : alphas np.argmin single split scores :.4f " k fold cross validation demo Leave-one-out CV LOOCV LOOCV is MATH -fold with MATH : each iteration holds out a single point. MATH Advantages: each training set has MATH points, so the estimate of test error is nearly unbiased. Costs: you train MATH times unless the hat-matrix shortcut applies , and variance can be surprisingly high because the MATH training sets share MATH identical points—so their errors are strongly positively correlated! When to use it: small MATH say, under 100 and fast models linear/ridge methods . python from sklearn.model selection import LeaveOneOut def compare cv methods : """5-fold CV and LOOCV on a small regression problem.""" np.random.seed 42 X, y = make regression n samples=50, n features=3, noise=5 alphas = np.logspace -1, 2, 15 kfold scores = for alpha in alphas: model = Ridge alpha=alpha scores = cross val score model, X, y, cv=5, scoring='neg mean squared error' kfold scores.append -scores.mean loo = LeaveOneOut loocv scores = for alpha in alphas: model = Ridge alpha=alpha scores = cross val score model, X, y, cv=loo, scoring='neg mean squared error' loocv scores.append -scores.mean plt.figure figsize= 10, 6 plt.semilogx alphas, kfold scores, 'o-', label='5-fold CV', linewidth=2 plt.semilogx alphas, loocv scores, 's-', label='LOOCV', linewidth=2 plt.xlabel 'α' plt.ylabel 'CV error' plt.title '5-fold CV vs LOOCV' plt.legend plt.grid True, alpha=0.3 plt.show print f"Optimal α 5-fold : alphas np.argmin kfold scores :.4f " print f"Optimal α LOOCV : alphas np.argmin loocv scores :.4f " compare cv methods Stratified MATH -fold classification With imbalanced classes, a plain random fold can accidentally contain almost no minority labels. Stratified MATH -fold keeps the class mix in each fold closely matched to the full sample. python from sklearn.model selection import StratifiedKFold from sklearn.datasets import make classification from sklearn.linear model import LogisticRegression def stratified cv demo : """Show class balance and accuracy under ordinary vs stratified folds.""" X, y = make classification n samples=100, n features=5, n informative=3, n redundant=0, weights= 0.8, 0.2 , random state=42 print f"Overall share of class 1: y.mean :.2% " print print "Ordinary K-fold:" kf = KFold n splits=5, shuffle=True, random state=42 for i, train idx, val idx in enumerate kf.split X : print f" Fold i + 1 : y val idx .mean :.2% class 1" print "\nStratified K-fold:" skf = StratifiedKFold n splits=5, shuffle=True, random state=42 for i, train idx, val idx in enumerate skf.split X, y : print f" Fold i + 1 : y val idx .mean :.2% class 1" model = LogisticRegression regular scores = cross val score model, X, y, cv=KFold n splits=5, shuffle=True, random state=42 stratified scores = cross val score model, X, y, cv=StratifiedKFold n splits=5, shuffle=True, random state=42 print f"\nOrdinary CV accuracy: regular scores.mean :.4f ± regular scores.std :.4f " print f"Stratified CV accuracy: stratified scores.mean :.4f ± stratified scores.std :.4f " stratified cv demo Bootstrap The bootstrap is another resampling device, especially powerful for measuring estimator uncertainty and out-of-bag error. Algorithm: 1. From MATH observations, draw MATH points with replacement a bootstrap sample . 2. Train on that sample. 3. Score the points that were not drawn out-of-bag , OOB . 4. Repeat MATH times often MATH or MATH . Bootstrap estimate of test error: MATH where MATH is the out-of-bag set for replicate MATH . --- Worked Example 2: The Famous MATH Out-of-Bag Rule by Hand When you draw MATH observations with replacement from a dataset of size MATH , what fraction of observations are left untouched out-of-bag for validation? For any fixed observation MATH : - On a single draw, the chance of missing observation MATH is MATH . - Across MATH independent draws, the probability that observation MATH is never picked is: MATH Plug in sample sizes MATH : - MATH : MATH out-of-bag. - MATH : MATH out-of-bag. - MATH : MATH out-of-bag. - MATH : MATH ! Every bootstrap sample contains roughly 63.2% unique observations with duplicates filling the remaining 36.8% slots , leaving 36.8% as a free built-in validation set! Because each bootstrap model trains on only ~63.2% unique data smaller effective sample size than full MATH , raw OOB error tends to be slightly pessimistic higher bias than 10-fold CV —which is why methods like the .632 bootstrap blend training and OOB error. --- python def bootstrap error estimation n bootstrap=100 : """Out-of-bag error versus 5-fold CV for Ridge.""" np.random.seed 42 X, y = make regression n samples=100, n features=5, noise=10 n samples = len X oob errors = for in range n bootstrap : bootstrap idx = np.random.choice n samples, size=n samples, replace=True oob idx = np.array i for i in range n samples if i not in bootstrap idx if len oob idx == 0: continue model = Ridge alpha=1.0 model.fit X bootstrap idx , y bootstrap idx pred oob = model.predict X oob idx oob errors.append np.mean y oob idx - pred oob 2 bootstrap estimate = np.mean oob errors cv scores = cross val score Ridge alpha=1.0 , X, y, cv=5, scoring='neg mean squared error' cv estimate = -cv scores.mean print f"Bootstrap estimate of test error: bootstrap estimate:.4f " print f"5-fold CV estimate: cv estimate:.4f " plt.figure figsize= 10, 6 plt.hist oob errors, bins=30, alpha=0.7, edgecolor='black' plt.axvline bootstrap estimate, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=2, label=f'Mean = bootstrap estimate:.4f ' plt.xlabel 'Out-of-bag error' plt.ylabel 'Frequency' plt.title f'Bootstrap error distribution n bootstrap iterations ' plt.legend plt.grid True, alpha=0.3 plt.show bootstrap error estimation --- Explanation: Why 5-Fold and 10-Fold Beat Both Single Splits and LOOCV Why do experienced practitioners almost always default to MATH or MATH instead of MATH or MATH LOOCV ? Follow these four steps slowly. Step 1: Small MATH like MATH suffers from pessimistic bias In 2-fold CV, every model trains on only MATH of the data. If the learning curve is still steep at MATH , the 2-fold error reflects a weaker, half-data model—systematically overestimating the error of your final full-data model. Step 2: Large MATH LOOCV, MATH removes bias—but inflates correlation! In LOOCV, every fold trains on MATH points, so bias virtually disappears. Yet any two LOOCV training sets share MATH identical points! Averaging MATH highly correlated numbers does not shrink variance like averaging MATH independent numbers does: MATH ! Step 3: Why MATH or MATH hits the sweet spot With MATH 80% train or MATH 90% train , each fold is large enough that bias is small, while the training folds differ enough to keep fold-to-fold correlation moderate—and you pay only 5–10 model fits instead of MATH . Step 4: When you tune hyperparameters, nest the loop! If you test 50 candidate hyperparameters with 5-fold CV and report the winning CV score as your final accuracy, that score is optimistically biased by selection. Nested CV wraps hyperparameter tuning inside an inner CV loop and evaluates the whole tuning procedure on an untouched outer CV loop. --- Which method when? | Method | Typical use | Strength | Weakness | |--------|-------------|----------|----------| | Train/test split | Quick baseline | Fast, simple | High variance | | 5-fold CV | Default for most tables | Bias–variance compromise | Slight pessimistic bias on tiny MATH | | 10-fold CV | Moderate MATH | Lower bias than 5-fold | MATH slower than 5-fold | | LOOCV | Small MATH MATH | Lowest bias | High fold correlation & slow | | Stratified CV | Imbalanced classification | Preserves class mix | Classification only | | Bootstrap | Uncertainty estimates / CIs | Flexible, distribution-free | Slight OOB pessimism 63.2% unique | Video tham khảo - Machine Learning Fundamentals: Cross Validation https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fSytzGwwBVw — StatQuest with Josh Starmer, English. xem trước. title: 01-08-00 Model Selection Criteria
content: Add a completely useless random column—say, the last digit of each customer’s phone number—to a linear regression, and watch what happens to ordinary MATH : it never goes down , and it almost always ticks slightly up ! Every extra parameter hands the model one more degree of freedom to absorb random training noise. Left unchecked, raw likelihood or MATH will always crown the bloated, overfitted monster. Cross-validation fights this empirically by holding out data. Information criteria —led by AIC , BIC , Adjusted MATH , and Mallows’ MATH —fight it analytically : they compute the exact mathematical “tax” you must charge for each extra parameter so that model selection rests on a principled formula rather than guesswork. --- Key ideas: Where Do Information Criteria Come From? Model selection criteria look like simple one-line formulas, yet they descend from three deep branches of statistical theory. 1. Information Theory & Kullback–Leibler Divergence AIC In 1974, Hirotugu Akaike asked: how close is our fitted probability distribution MATH to the unknown true data-generating distribution MATH ? Measuring closeness by Kullback–Leibler KL divergence , he proved that the maximized log-likelihood MATH is optimistically biased by approximately MATH the number of fitted parameters —producing AIC MATH . - Core questions: Which candidate model will predict new observations most accurately minimizing out-of-sample KL loss ? - Real-world reach: Time-series ARIMA order selection, ecological modeling, and generalized linear model comparison. 2. Bayesian Model Comparison & Laplace Approximation BIC In 1978, Gideon Schwarz approached model selection from a completely different philosophy: which model has the highest posterior probability MATH ? Integrating over parameter space via Laplace’s approximation yields BIC MATH —charging a penalty that grows with sample size MATH . - Core questions: If the true sparse model sits inside our candidate list, which criterion guarantees we recover it as MATH model-selection consistency ? - Real-world reach: Choosing the number of clusters in Gaussian Mixture Models GMMs , phylogenetic trees, and structural econometrics. 3. Degrees of Freedom & Unbiased Risk Estimation Adjusted MATH & Mallows’ MATH In classical Gaussian linear regression, training residual sum of squares MATH underestimates expected squared prediction error by MATH . Adding back MATH produces Mallows’ MATH , while dividing sums of squares by their respective degrees of freedom MATH vs. MATH produces Adjusted MATH . - Core questions: When does an extra predictor genuinely reduce noise variance rather than merely consuming a degree of freedom? - Real-world reach: Variable screening in linear regression and subset-selection diagnostics. --- The selection problem The basic tradeoff: - A rich model fits training data tightly, risking high variance overfitting . - A parsimonious model risks bias underfitting , yet often generalizes more reliably. Every selection criterion below has the same two-part anatomy: MATH Akaike information criterion AIC AIC estimates relative out-of-sample prediction error up to a constant : MATH where MATH is the maximized likelihood and MATH is the number of estimated parameters. Rule: prefer the smaller AIC. title: 01-10-00 A Practical Machine Learning Workflow
content:
Ask a veteran data scientist why real-world machine learning projects fail in production, and they will almost never blame the math of Ridge regression or Random Forests. They will tell you stories about data leakage —scaling a dataset before splitting off the test set, tuning hyperparameters on the final exam, or dropping outliers using global statistics that quietly peeked into the future. A model can post a dazzling MATH inside a Jupyter notebook and collapse the day it meets real customers simply because the pipeline violated basic experimental hygiene. Earlier lessons introduced individual statistical tools one at a time. This lesson assembles them into a disciplined, end-to-end eight-step workflow on the California Housing dataset—from exploratory data analysis and leak-free preprocessing through baselines, cross-validated tuning, one-shot test evaluation, and residual diagnostics. --- Key ideas: What Statistical Principles Govern an ML Pipeline? A clean pipeline is not bureaucratic boilerplate—every step defends against a specific statistical failure mode. 1. Exploratory Data Analysis EDA & Robust Preprocessing Before fitting any equation, EDA checks distributions, missingness, skewness, and extreme outliers. Skewed features like population or income stretch linear losses disproportionately; log transforms np.log1p and IQR outlier checks stabilize variance and prevent a handful of anomalous rows from hijacking parameter estimates. - Core questions: Are features on wildly different scales? Are target values censored or heavy-tailed? - Real-world reach: Financial fraud detection, real-estate pricing, clinical lab measurements, and sensor telemetry. 2. Data Splitting, Information Barriers & Leakage Prevention Statistical generalization requires the test set to act as an independent draw from the unseen future population. Any step that learns parameters from data—computing means/standard deviations StandardScaler , imputing medians, selecting features, or picking hyperparameters— must be fitted strictly inside the training split wrapped in a Pipeline , never across the full dataset. - Core questions: Which steps are “stateless” row transformations versus “stateful” estimators that can leak test information? - Real-world reach: Reproducible clinical trials, quantitative trading backtests preventing look-ahead bias , and production ML platforms. 3. Multi-Metric Evaluation & Residual Diagnostics A single summary number like MSE can hide systematic bias, heteroscedasticity error growing with predicted value , or sensitivity to a single bad prediction. Pairing RMSE , MAE , and MATH with residual plots reveals whether your model genuinely captured the signal or left structured patterns behind. - Core questions: Are residuals centered near zero with roughly constant spread? Where does the model systematically under- or over-predict? - Real-world reach: Model auditing, regulatory validation in banking/healthcare, and iterative error analysis. --- An end-to-end outline A disciplined project walks through eight steps in strict order: 1. Problem understanding and EDA 2. Data preprocessing 3. Feature engineering 4. Train / validation / test split 5. A baseline model 6. Model selection and hyperparameter tuning 7. Final evaluation touch the test set once 8. Interpretation and residual diagnostics --- Worked Example 1: Catching Data Leakage by Hand on a 5-Point Dataset Why is calling StandardScaler .fit transform X before train test split such a serious mistake? Watch what happens on five tiny house-size measurements: MATH 1. WRONG Leaky — scale all 5 points together first : - Combined mean: MATH . - Combined standard deviation: MATH . - Standardized training values become MATH —every single normal house looks negative because the unseen test mansion silently dragged the mean up from 13 to 30.4! 2. RIGHT Leak-free — fit scaler on Train only, transform Test using Train’s MATH : - Training mean: MATH , training std: MATH . - Standardized training values: MATH cleanly centered! . - Standardized test value: MATH —honestly flagging the test mansion as an extreme outlier, exactly as it would appear in live production! Rule of thumb: Always split first , or wrap StandardScaler inside a scikit-learn Pipeline so GridSearchCV re-fits the scaler fresh inside every cross-validation fold. --- python import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns from sklearn.model selection import train test split, GridSearchCV, cross val score from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.linear model import Ridge, Lasso, LogisticRegression from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.metrics import mean squared error, r2 score import warnings warnings.filterwarnings 'ignore' sns.set style 'whitegrid' plt.rcParams 'figure.figsize' = 10, 6 Step 1: Understand the problem and explore the data python from sklearn.datasets import fetch california housing def load and explore data : """Load California housing and run a lightweight EDA.""" housing = fetch california housing as frame=True df = housing.frame print "=" 60 print "DATA SUMMARY" print "=" 60 print f"Number of samples: len df " print f"Number of features: len df.columns - 1 " print f"

X = df.drop 'MedHouseVal', axis=1 y = df 'MedHouseVal' def remove outliers data, column, threshold=3 : Q1 = data column .quantile 0.25 Q3 = data column .quantile 0.75 IQR = Q3 - Q1 lower = Q1 - threshold IQR upper = Q3 + threshold IQR return data data column >= lower & data column 	ext MAE MATH +0.5 MATH more heavily! 4. MATH : Total sum of squares MATH ; residual sum of squares MATH ; so MATH --- python def final evaluation best model, preprocessor, X test, y test : """Report test metrics and residual diagnostics.""" X test scaled = preprocessor.transform X test y pred = best model.predict X test scaled mse = mean squared error y test, y pred rmse = np.sqrt mse r2 = r2 score y test, y pred mae = np.mean np.abs y test - y pred print "=" 60 print "FINAL TEST SET PERFORMANCE" print "=" 60 print f"MSE: mse:.4f " print f"RMSE: rmse:.4f " print f"MAE: mae:.4f " print f"R²: r2:.4f " fig, axes = plt.subplots 1, 2, figsize= 14, 5 axes 0 .scatter y test, y pred, alpha=0.3, s=10 axes 0 .plot y test.min , y test.max , y test.min , y test.max , 'r--', linewidth=2, label='Perfect prediction' axes 0 .set xlabel 'Actual values' axes 0 .set ylabel 'Predicted values' axes 0 .set title 'Predicted vs actual' axes 0 .legend axes 0 .grid True, alpha=0.3 residuals = y test - y pred axes 1 .scatter y pred, residuals, alpha=0.3, s=10 axes 1 .axhline y=0, color='r', linestyle='--', linewidth=2 axes 1 .set xlabel 'Predicted values' axes 1 .set ylabel 'Residuals' axes 1 .set title 'Residual plot' axes 1 .grid True, alpha=0.3 plt.tight layout plt.show final evaluation results best name 'model' , preprocessor, X test, y test Step 8: Interpret python def interpret model model, feature names : """Plot coefficients or impurity-based importances when they exist.""" if hasattr model, 'coef ' : importances = np.abs model.coef title = 'Absolute feature coefficients' elif hasattr model, 'feature importances ' : importances = model.feature importances title = 'Feature importances' else: print "This model does not expose a simple importance vector." return indices = np.argsort importances ::-1 plt.figure figsize= 10, 6 plt.barh range len importances , importances indices , align='center' plt.yticks range len importances , feature names i for i in indices plt.xlabel 'Importance' plt.title title plt.gca .invert yaxis plt.tight layout plt.show print "
Top 5 features:" for i in range min 5, len importances : idx = indices i print f" i + 1 . feature names idx :20s : importances idx :.4f " interpret model results best name 'model' , X train.columns.tolist One function that runs the whole path python def complete ml workflow : """Execute steps 1–8 in sequence.""" print "STEP 1: LOAD & EXPLORE DATA" print "=" 60 df = load and explore data print "

STEP 2: PREPROCESSING" print "=" 60 X, y = preprocess data df print "

STEP 3: FEATURE ENGINEERING" print "=" 60 X eng = create features X print "

STEP 4: TRAIN / VAL / TEST SPLIT" print "=" 60 X train, X val, X test, y train, y val, y test = split data X eng, y print "

STEP 5: BASELINE MODEL" print "=" 60 baseline mse = build baseline X train, y train, X val, y val print "

STEP 6: MODEL SELECTION & TUNING" print "=" 60 results, best name, preprocessor = model selection pipeline X train, y train, X val, y val print "

STEP 7: FINAL EVALUATION" print "=" 60 final evaluation results best name 'model' , preprocessor, X test, y test print "

STEP 8: MODEL INTERPRETATION" print "=" 60 interpret model results best name 'model' , X train.columns.tolist return results, best name results, best model name = complete ml workflow --- Explanation: Why Three Splits and One Final Test Are Non-Negotiable Why not save data by splitting only into Train and Test, tuning your hyperparameters on Test, and reporting the best score? Follow these four steps slowly. Step 1: Every time you pick a winner on a dataset, you fit to its noise Suppose you evaluate 100 random models on the same validation set. Even if every single model has identical true error, the luckiest model on that finite validation set will look noticeably better than average—a statistical bias called selection optimism the winner’s curse . Step 2: That is why Validation gets “spent” during model selection Once you use the validation set to pick between Ridge, Lasso, and Random Forest and their hyperparameters , the validation score is no longer an unbiased estimate of future performance—it has been used to make decisions! Step 3: The Test set is your sealed envelope By locking the test set away until every preprocessing rule, feature, model family, and hyperparameter is frozen, evaluating on Test once gives an honest, unbiased measurement of generalization error. If you peek at Test and go back to tweak the model, you have just turned Test into a second Validation set. Step 4: Spot the subtle leakage still hiding in our prototype above! Look closely at Step 2 preprocess data in our script above: it trimmed outliers across df before splitting, and Step 6 fit StandardScaler once on X train outside GridSearchCV ! In Exercise 3 below, wrapping preprocessing inside a scikit-learn Pipeline fixes that subtle fold-to-fold leakage completely—an essential upgrade for production-grade ML. --- A short checklist Data understanding. Do a real EDA. Look for missing values, outliers, and skewed features. Splitting. Cut train / validation / test before you transform anything. Do not look at the test set until the end. Preprocessing. Fit on train, transform on validation and test. Prefer a Pipeline so leakage is harder. Selection. Start from a dumb baseline, compare several models, and use cross-validation. Tuning. GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV on the validation side—never on the test set. Final evaluation. Score the test set once. Report more than one metric MSE, MATH , MAE, … . Interpretation. Feature importance, residual plots, and a sentence about why the model works. The lesson encodes categories with OneHotEncoder; this video explains one-hot before the other encodings. - Machine Learning Tutorial Python - 16: Hyper parameter Tuning GridSearchCV https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HdlDYng8g9s — codebasics, English. GridSearchCV in scikit-learn for the hyperparameter step of the case study. Exercises Exercise 1: End-to-end project. Run the full workflow on the diabetes data or another regression table . Compare at least three models. Exercise 2: Feature engineering. Invent at least five extra features for California housing and check whether they help. Exercise 3: Pipeline automation. Wrap preprocessing, feature construction, and training in a single scikit-learn Pipeline .

title: 01-11-00 Applications and recent developments
content: It is tempting to treat Monte Carlo, cross-validation, and model selection as warm-up exercises you leave behind once “real” deep learning begins. In reality, they have become the exact working language of frontier AI evaluation and uncertainty quantification. When you deploy a black-box neural network in a hospital, rank large language models on Chatbot Arena, or report cross-validation error in a top journal, there is no neat closed-form Gaussian formula to save you—only resampling , empirical quantiles , and paired-comparison estimation . This optional note connects Chapter 01’s core toolkit to three major 2022–2024 breakthroughs: split conformal prediction , Monte Carlo / Bradley–Terry evaluation of LLMs , and what cross-validation actually estimates . --- Key ideas: How Chapter 01 Tools Power Modern AI Evaluation Three statistical themes tie these recent papers directly back to our opening lessons. 1. Distribution-Free Uncertainty Conformal Prediction Classical confidence intervals assume Gaussian errors or large-sample asymptotics. Conformal prediction uses a held-out calibration split and order statistics to wrap any black-box predictor tree, neural net, LLM in a prediction set MATH with a finite-sample coverage guarantee—relying only on exchangeability . - Core questions: How can we guarantee MATH without assuming the model is correctly specified? - Real-world reach: Clinical decision support, autonomous-driving perception bounds, and financial forecasting intervals. 2. Paired-Comparison Modeling & Multi-Scenario Simulation LLM Benchmarks Evaluating open-ended language models has no closed-form accuracy. HELM treats evaluation as a multi-scenario Monte Carlo design across seven metrics, while Chatbot Arena uses the Bradley–Terry logistic model to turn anonymous pairwise human votes into calibrated strength ratings with bootstrap confidence intervals. - Core questions: How do we separate genuine model improvement from benchmark sampling noise? - Real-world reach: Public LLM leaderboards LMSYS Chatbot Arena , A/B ranking of search/recommendation systems, and sports rating engines Elo . 3. Honest Resampling Inference Nested Cross-Validation Standard MATH -fold CV reuses every point for both training and validation, creating subtle correlations across folds. Recent theoretical work Bates, Hastie, Tibshirani, JASA 2023 clarified which error CV estimates and why nested CV is required for valid confidence intervals around generalization error. - Core questions: Does CV estimate the error of my specific fitted model or the average error of the fitting algorithm ? - Real-world reach: High-stakes benchmark reporting, AutoML model selection, and reproducible ML papers. --- Conformal prediction as a hold-out Monte Carlo A classifier or regressor MATH typically returns a single point MATH . High-stakes settings diagnostics, ranking, content moderation need a set MATH that covers the true label with a user-chosen probability MATH . Split conformal prediction does this with the exact same computational idea as a validation split: fit MATH on a training fold; on a disjoint calibration fold of size MATH compute nonconformity scores MATH for example, absolute residuals MATH ; then take the finite-sample corrected empirical quantile MATH \hat q = \text Quantile \frac \lceil n+1 1-\alpha \rceil n \bigl s 1,\ldots,s n\bigr . MATH The prediction set MATH then satisfies, under exchangeability alone, MATH P\bigl Y n+1 \in C X n+1 \bigr \ge 1 - \alpha. MATH No Gaussian residual, no correctly specified model—only the exchangeability that also justifies ordinary cross-validation. Angelopoulos and Bates’s monograph Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning , 2023; arXiv:2107.07511 https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07511 is the formulation most 2023–2026 software cites, and the scikit-learn-contrib library MAPIE https://mapie.readthedocs.io/ Cordier, Blot, Lacombe, Morzadec, Capitaine, Brunel, COPA 2023 wraps the same quantile around any estimator. --- Worked Example 1: Building a 90% Conformal Prediction Interval by Hand Suppose your regression model predicts house prices on a tiny calibration fold of MATH unseen houses, producing sorted absolute residuals MATH in $10k : MATH You want a 90% coverage guarantee MATH for a brand-new house MATH whose point prediction is MATH : 1. Compute the conformal rank index: MATH 2. Read the 9th sorted residual: MATH . 3. Output the prediction interval: MATH Why does this guarantee MATH coverage? Because all 10 residuals MATH are exchangeable, the new residual MATH is equally likely to land in any of the 10 rank positions! The chance it lands in positions 1 through 9 i.e., MATH is at least MATH —even if your regression model is nonlinear, biased, or completely non-Gaussian! --- Simulation for LLM evaluation There is no closed-form accuracy for a chat model. Liang, Bommasani, Lee, and colleagues Holistic Evaluation of Language Models , TMLR 2023 https://openreview.net/forum?id=iO4LZibEqW ; arXiv:2211.09110 https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110 ; toolkit stanford-crfm/helm https://github.com/stanford-crfm/helm treat evaluation as a designed experiment: 16 core scenarios, seven metrics accuracy, calibration , robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency , and 30 models run under a shared protocol. The Law of Large Numbers from our opening lesson is what makes a multi-scenario average meaningful; a single headline number is a noisy one-draw Monte Carlo. Human preference is even less analytic. Chiang, Zheng, Sheng, Angelopoulos, Li, Li, Zhu, Zhang, Jordan, Gonzalez, and Stoica Chatbot Arena , ICML 2024 https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/chiang24b.html ; arXiv:2403.04132 https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04132 collect anonymous pairwise votes and estimate a Bradley–Terry strength MATH for each model. If model MATH beats model MATH with probability MATH P i \succ j = \frac e^ \theta i e^ \theta i +e^ \theta j = \frac 1 1 + e^ - \theta i - \theta j , MATH then leaderboard ranking is a statistical estimation problem, not a fixed trophy table. Bootstrap confidence intervals and adaptive pair sampling turn raw vote counts into honest uncertainty bars. --- Worked Example 2: Bradley–Terry Win Probabilities & Arena Elo Ratings by Hand Suppose Chatbot Arena estimates latent strengths MATH and MATH for two LLMs: 1. Predicted win probability of Model A over Model B: MATH 2. Converting to the Chess/Arena Elo scale where 400 Elo points correspond to a MATH win odds ratio, so MATH : A gap of MATH equals MATH Elo points ! Conversely, a narrow leaderboard lead of just 10 Elo points corresponds to MATH , or a win probability of only MATH —explaining why small Elo gaps with overlapping bootstrap intervals are statistically indistinguishable! --- What cross-validation actually estimates The Chapter 01 CV lesson treats the CV score as an estimate of test error for “the” fitted model. Bates, Hastie, and Tibshirani Journal of the American Statistical Association , 2023; PMC11412612 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11412612/ prove that, already for ordinary least squares, MATH -fold CV estimates the average prediction error of models trained on random draws of the training set—not the error of the specific MATH you will ship. Fold-wise errors are correlated each point is used for both training and testing , so a naïve standard error is too small and the usual confidence interval undercovers. Their remedy is a nested CV used specifically to estimate that variance cleanly. python import numpy as np from sklearn.datasets import make regression from sklearn.linear model import Ridge from sklearn.model selection import KFold, GridSearchCV, cross val score X, y = make regression n samples=200, n features=20, noise=8.0, random state=0 inner = KFold n splits=5, shuffle=True, random state=0 outer = KFold n splits=5, shuffle=True, random state=1 search = GridSearchCV Ridge , "alpha": np.logspace -2, 2, 9 , cv=inner Outer CV estimates prediction error of the selection procedure , not of one alpha. scores = cross val score search, X, y, cv=outer print "nested CV mean:", scores.mean , "sd:", scores.std ddof=1 That snippet does not claim a new theorem. It is the Bates–Hastie–Tibshirani distinction in code: the quantity you report is an average over re-fitted, re-tuned models. --- Explanation: Why Exchangeability Unifies Conformal, Arena, and Nested CV These three 2022–2024 breakthroughs look completely different on the surface, yet they obey the exact same four-step statistical discipline. Step 1: Never trust a single point estimate without a distribution or interval A point prediction MATH hides how uncertain the model is; a single Arena Elo rank hides how few head-to-head votes separate 2 from 3; a single GridSearchCV.best score hides selection optimism. Step 2: Replace fragile parametric assumptions with resampling & order statistics Instead of assuming residuals are Gaussian which fails on multimodal or heavy-tailed AI outputs , split conformal prediction relies solely on exchangeability of calibration and test points—and Chatbot Arena uses nonparametric bootstrap resampling over vote pairs. Step 3: Guard the boundary between fitting and evaluating Split conformal requires the calibration fold to be completely untouched during training; nested CV requires the outer test fold to be untouched during hyperparameter tuning. Cross that boundary even once, and your mathematical guarantee evaporates. Step 4: Remember what breaks when the world drifts Every guarantee above assumes tomorrow’s test data come from the same distribution as today’s calibration/CV data exchangeability . Under distribution shift new user demographics, new prompt styles, market regime change , even conformal coverage can drop—which is why adaptive conformal inference and continuous monitoring are active frontiers today. --- What to carry forward When a paper says “we conformalize a black-box,” “we report Arena scores with intervals,” or “we nest the tuner,” it is speaking Chapter 01. Later lectures add random variables and hypothesis tests; they do not replace simulation, resampling, or the habit of asking which error a criterion estimates. Angelopoulos teaches split conformal prediction: nonconformity scores on a calibration set, then a quantile — the procedure this note ties to arXiv:2107.07511. - Holistic Evaluation of Language Models HELM - Yifan Mai, Stanford University https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fLoYcXLG6ro — PyTorch, English. Yifan Mai presents HELM, the multi-scenario evaluation this note reads as a Monte Carlo experiment for language models. - 11.5 Nested CV for Algorithm Selection L11 Model Eval. title: Bài 1: Các Loại Dữ Liệu và Đặc Trưng
content:
Nếu ai đó cộng mã bưu điện của TP. Hồ Chí Minh 70000 với Hà Nội 10000 rồi chia đôi để kết luận "mã bưu điện trung bình của hai thành phố là 40000 ", hẳn bạn sẽ bật cười vì sự vô nghĩa đó. Thế nhưng trong phân tích dữ liệu thực tế, rất nhiều lỗi ngớ ngẩn lại xảy ra theo đúng kiểu ấy — chỉ tinh vi hơn một chút: lấy trung bình số sao đánh giá 1–5 rồi xem khoảng cách từ 1 lên 2 sao bằng hệt khoảng cách từ 4 lên 5 sao, hay tuyên bố hôm nay MATH "nóng gấp đôi" hôm qua MATH ! Mọi công cụ thống kê — từ trung bình, trung vị, biểu đồ cột đến mô hình học máy — đều chỉ có ý nghĩa khi ta tôn trọng bản chất và thang đo của dữ liệu . Bài học mở đầu Chương 2 giúp bạn phân loại rạch ròi từng kiểu dữ liệu trước khi thực hiện bất kỳ phép tính nào. --- Kiến thức cần nhớ: Thang đo dữ liệu NOIR là gì và nghiên cứu những gì? Trong thống kê mô tả, dữ liệu được tổ chức theo hai trục: Định tính vs. Định lượng rời rạc/liên tục và 4 thang đo kinh điển của Stevens NOIR — mỗi nấc mở khóa thêm một nhóm phép toán hợp lệ: 1. Định danh Nominal : Chỉ phân loại nhãn không có thứ tự màu mắt, tỉnh thành, mã sản phẩm → chỉ hợp lệ phép đếm tần suất và Mode . 2. Thứ bậc Ordinal : Có thứ tự rõ ràng nhưng khoảng cách giữa các bậc không nhất thiết bằng nhau xếp hạng 1–5 sao, mức độ hài lòng → thêm được Trung vị Median và phân vị . 3. Khoảng Interval : Hiệu số giữa hai giá trị có ý nghĩa vật lý đều nhau, nhưng số 0 là quy ước tùy ý nhiệt độ MATH , năm dương lịch → cộng/trừ và Trung bình hợp lệ, nhưng phép chia tỷ số vô nghĩa . 4. Tỷ lệ Ratio : Có điểm 0 tuyệt đối thu nhập, chiều cao, thời gian, nhiệt độ Kelvin → mọi phép toán cộng, trừ, nhân, chia tỷ số đều hợp lệ. --- 1. Mục tiêu bài học Sau khi hoàn thành bài học này, người học có thể: - Phân biệt rõ giữa dữ liệu định tính qualitative và định lượng quantitative . - Nhận diện bốn thang đo dữ liệu: định danh Nominal , thứ bậc Ordinal , khoảng Interval và tỷ lệ Ratio . - Phân biệt dữ liệu rời rạc discrete với dữ liệu liên tục continuous . - Sử dụng Python Pandas để kiểm tra và chuyển đổi kiểu dữ liệu trong thực tế. 2. Kiến thức tiền đề - Kiến thức cơ bản về lập trình Python. - Thao tác cơ bản với thư viện pandas . 3. Động lực và giới thiệu Hãy xét một tình huống quen thuộc trong thương mại điện tử: bạn nhận được tập dữ liệu khách hàng gồm độ tuổi, thu nhập, điểm đánh giá sản phẩm 1–5 sao và hạng thẻ thành viên Vàng, Bạc, Đồng . Nếu tính trung bình cộng của "hạng thẻ thành viên", kết quả sẽ không có ý nghĩa vì đây là dữ liệu định tính có thứ bậc, không phải đại lượng số học. Ngược lại, tính trung bình của "thu nhập" lại hoàn toàn hợp lý. Xác định đúng loại dữ liệu là bước nền tảng để chọn phương pháp thống kê và thuật toán học máy phù hợp; sai sót ngay từ bước này sẽ dẫn đến kết quả phân tích sai lệch "Garbage In, Garbage Out" . 4. Các khái niệm cốt lõi và lý thuyết 4.1 Phân loại dữ liệu Data Types Dữ liệu thống kê thường được chia thành hai nhóm chính: 1. Dữ liệu định tính Qualitative / Categorical Data : - Mô tả thuộc tính hoặc nhãn phân loại, không biểu diễn đại lượng đo lường theo nghĩa số học. - Ví dụ: giới tính Nam/Nữ , màu sắc Đỏ/Xanh/Vàng , mã bưu điện. 2. Dữ liệu định lượng Quantitative / Numerical Data : - Biểu diễn bằng giá trị số, cho phép thực hiện các phép toán số học +, -, , / . - Gồm hai loại: - Rời rạc Discrete : Nhận các giá trị đếm được, hữu hạn hoặc vô hạn đếm được ví dụ: số con trong gia đình, số lỗi trong một đoạn mã . - Liên tục Continuous : Có thể nhận bất kỳ giá trị nào trong một khoảng số thực ví dụ: chiều cao, cân nặng, nhiệt độ . 4.2 Thang đo dữ liệu Levels of Measurement Xác định đúng thang đo giúp biết phép toán và thước đo thống kê nào hợp lệ: | Thang đo Level | Đặc điểm | Ví dụ | Phép toán hợp lệ | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Định danh Nominal | Dùng để gọi tên và phân loại; thứ tự giữa các nhãn không có ý nghĩa. | Giới tính, tên thành phố, màu mắt. | Đếm tần số Frequency , yếu vị Mode . Không so sánh lớn hơn/nhỏ hơn. | | Thứ bậc Ordinal | Có thứ tự rõ ràng, nhưng khoảng cách giữa các bậc không xác định hoặc không đều nhau. | Xếp hạng phim 1–5 sao , trình độ học vấn Cử nhân, Thạc sĩ, Tiến sĩ . | So sánh thứ tự Rank , trung vị Median . Không cộng trừ trực tiếp. | | Khoảng Interval | Có thứ tự, khoảng cách giữa các giá trị đều nhau và có ý nghĩa, nhưng không có điểm 0 tuyệt đối giá trị 0 không có nghĩa là "không có gì" . | Nhiệt độ °C, °F , năm lịch. | Cộng, trừ, tính trung bình Mean . Không lấy tỷ số 40°C không nóng gấp đôi 20°C . | | Tỷ lệ Ratio | Có đầy đủ tính chất của thang đo khoảng và có điểm 0 tuyệt đối, nên tỷ số có ý nghĩa. | Chiều cao, cân nặng, thu nhập, thời gian. | Mọi phép toán +, -, , / ; ví dụ 100g nặng gấp đôi 50g. | 5. Ví dụ minh họa Ví dụ 1: Phân loại biến số Xét các biến số sau trong một khảo sát y tế: 1. Nhóm máu A, B, AB, O : Định tính, thang đo định danh. 2. Mức độ đau Nhẹ, Vừa, Nặng : Định tính, thang đo thứ bậc. 3. Nhiệt độ cơ thể °C : Định lượng, liên tục, thang đo khoảng. 4. Số nhịp tim mỗi phút : Định lượng, rời rạc, thang đo tỷ lệ. 6. Triển khai trên Python Thư viện pandas hỗ trợ quản lý các kiểu dữ liệu tương ứng: - object hoặc category : thường dùng cho dữ liệu định tính. - int64 : thường dùng cho dữ liệu định lượng rời rạc. - float64 : thường dùng cho dữ liệu định lượng liên tục. python import pandas as pd import numpy as np Tạo một tập dữ liệu giả lập data = 'KhachHang ID': 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 , 'GioiTinh': 'Nam', 'Nu', 'Nu', 'Nam', 'Nu' , 'TrinhDo HocVan': 'CuNhan', 'TienSi', 'ThacSi', 'CuNhan', 'ThacSi' , 'Diem DanhGia': 4, 5, 3, 4, 1 , Thang đo 1-5 'ThuNhap HangThang Trieu': 15.5, 30.0, 22.5, 18.0, 25.0 , 'So Con': 0, 2, 1, 0, 3 df = pd.DataFrame data print "--- Xem dữ liệu thô ---" print df print "
--- Kiểu dữ liệu trong Pandas ---" print df.dtypes 1. Chuyển đổi GioiTinh sang kiểu Category Nominal df 'GioiTinh' = df 'GioiTinh' .astype 'category' 2. Chuyển đổi TrinhDo HocVan sang kiểu Category có thứ tự Ordinal trinh do order = 'CuNhan', 'ThacSi', 'TienSi' df 'TrinhDo HocVan' = pd.Categorical df 'TrinhDo HocVan' , categories=trinh do order, ordered=True print "
--- Sau khi chuyển đổi kiểu dữ liệu ---" print df.dtypes Kiểm tra thứ tự của biến Ordinal print "
--- So sánh biến Ordinal ---" print f"Thạc Sĩ > Cử Nhân: df.iloc 2 'TrinhDo HocVan' > df.iloc 0 'TrinhDo HocVan' " 3. Phân biệt Rời rạc và Liên tục So Con là rời rạc, ThuNhap là liên tục. Pandas thường lưu cả hai dưới dạng số int64/float64 , nhưng về mặt thống kê chúng ta xử lý khác nhau ví dụ khi vẽ biểu đồ . 7. Giải thích và các lỗi thường gặp Lỗi 1: Xử lý dữ liệu định danh hoặc thứ bậc như dữ liệu tỷ lệ - Sai lầm : Tính trung bình cộng cho mã bưu điện dữ liệu định danh hoặc xếp hạng sao dữ liệu thứ bậc mà không xét đến bản chất thang đo. - Giải thích : Mã bưu điện chỉ là nhãn định danh nên giá trị trung bình hoàn toàn vô nghĩa. Với xếp hạng sao, khoảng cách cảm nhận giữa "1 sao" và "2 sao" có thể không tương đương khoảng cách giữa "4 sao" và "5 sao". Trong thực tế phân tích dữ liệu, đôi khi thang đo Likert 1–5 vẫn được tính trung bình để tóm tắt nhanh, nhưng cần diễn giải thận trọng. Lỗi 2: Chọn sai biểu đồ cho kiểu dữ liệu - Sai lầm : Vẽ biểu đồ đường line plot cho dữ liệu danh mục không có thứ tự. - Hậu quả : Đường nối giữa các nhãn danh mục tạo cảm giác về một xu hướng liên tục không hề tồn tại. Giải thích: tự tay kiểm tra vì sao MATH KHÔNG "nóng gấp đôi" MATH Hãy kiểm chứng sự khác biệt giữa thang Khoảng Interval và thang Tỷ lệ Ratio bằng phép đổi đơn vị đơn giản: 1. Kiểm tra nhiệt độ Thang Khoảng : So sánh hai ngày MATH và MATH . - Tỷ số ngây thơ theo độ C: MATH "nóng gấp đôi"? . - Đổi sang thang đo vật lý tuyệt đối Kelvin MATH : MATH 20^\circ\mathrm C = 293.15\,\mathrm K , \qquad 40^\circ\mathrm C = 313.15\,\mathrm K \;\Longrightarrow\;  rac 313.15 293.15 \approx 1.068! MATH Năng lượng nhiệt thực tế chỉ tăng có 6.8% , hoàn toàn không phải 100%! Nguyên nhân: điểm MATH chỉ là nhiệt độ đóng băng của nước quy ước , không phải trạng thái "không có nhiệt". Trong khi đó, hiệu số MATH lại hoàn toàn bất biến! 2. Đối chiếu với thu nhập Thang Tỷ lệ : Thu nhập 20 triệu và 40 triệu VND. Đổi sang USD chia cho MATH ta được MATH USD và MATH USD — tỷ số MATH giữ nguyên bất biến vì 0 đồng thực sự có nghĩa là không có tiền! title: Bài 2: Các Đặc Trưng Số (Numerical Measures)
content: Một câu chuyện cười nổi tiếng trong giới thống kê kể rằng: có 9 người bình thường đang ngồi uống cà phê với thu nhập trung bình 15 triệu đồng/tháng. Bỗng một tỷ phú bước vào quán — ngay lập tức, thu nhập trung bình của cả quán vọt lên hàng trăm tỷ đồng , dù chẳng có ai trong 9 vị khách ban đầu giàu thêm một xu nào! Câu chuyện ấy tóm gọn linh hồn của bài học này: một bảng dữ liệu có hàng nghìn con số cần được nén lại thành vài đặc trưng số dễ hiểu, nhưng nếu bạn chỉ nhìn mỗi số "trung bình" mà quên đi trung vị median , độ lệch chuẩn SD và khoảng tứ phân vị IQR , những con số tóm tắt đó rất dễ nói dối bạn. --- Kiến thức cần nhớ: Các đặc trưng số trong thống kê mô tả đo những chiều kích nào? Để mô tả trọn vẹn một tập dữ liệu số mà không bị một con số đơn lẻ đánh lừa, thống kê mô tả luôn đi theo bốn trụ cột bổ trợ nhau : 1. Xu hướng trung tâm Center : Dữ liệu tụ quanh đâu? Gồm Trung bình Mean — nhạy với ngoại lai , Trung vị Median — vững chắc khi phân phối lệch và Yếu vị Mode — giá trị phổ biến nhất . 2. Độ phân tán Spread : Dữ liệu trải rộng hay tụ chặt? Gồm Phương sai Variance , Độ lệch chuẩn Standard Deviation — cùng đơn vị dữ liệu , và Khoảng tứ phân vị MATH — đo 50% dữ liệu ở giữa . 3. Vị trí tương đối & Hình dạng Position & Shape : Phân vị Percentiles , điểm chuẩn hóa MATH -score, độ lệch Skewness và độ nhọn Kurtosis . 4. Tính vững Robustness : Biết cặp đôi nào nhạy cảm với ngoại lai Mean + SD , tốt cho phân phối chuẩn đối xứng và cặp đôi nào miễn nhiễm với ngoại lai Median + IQR , bắt buộc dùng cho thu nhập, giá nhà hay dữ liệu đuôi nặng . --- 1. Mục tiêu bài học Sau khi hoàn thành bài học này, người học có thể: - Hiểu và tính toán các đại lượng đo khuynh hướng trung tâm Mean, Median, Mode . - Hiểu và tính toán các đại lượng đo mức độ phân tán Variance, Standard Deviation, Range, IQR . - Phân biệt tham số tổng thể Parameter với thống kê mẫu Statistic . - Sử dụng Python NumPy, Pandas để tính toán nhanh các đặc trưng số trên dữ liệu thực tế. 2. Kiến thức tiền đề - Bài 1: Các loại dữ liệu và đặc trưng. - Kiến thức Python cơ bản và thư viện numpy . 3. Động lực và giới thiệu Khi làm việc với một tập dữ liệu lớn gồm hàng triệu dòng, ta không thể đọc từng quan sát để nắm bắt thông tin mà cần các con số tóm tắt đại diện: - "Doanh thu trung bình tháng này là bao nhiêu?" → Trung bình cộng Mean . - "Mức lương chia đôi tập nhân viên thành hai nửa bằng nhau là bao nhiêu?" → Trung vị Median . - "Mức độ biến động của cổ phiếu này lớn hay nhỏ?" → Độ lệch chuẩn Standard Deviation — biến động càng cao, rủi ro càng lớn. Các đặc trưng số Numerical Measures là công cụ cơ bản của Thống kê Mô tả Descriptive Statistics . 4. Các khái niệm cốt lõi và lý thuyết 4.1 Khuynh hướng trung tâm Measures of Central Tendency Các đại lượng này mô tả vị trí trung tâm của phân phối dữ liệu: 1. Trung bình cộng Mean — MATH hoặc MATH : - Công thức mẫu: MATH . - Nhạy cảm với giá trị ngoại lai outliers . Chẳng hạn, nếu Elon Musk bước vào một quán bar, thu nhập trung bình của những người trong quán sẽ tăng vọt dù thu nhập thực tế của đa số mọi người không hề thay đổi. 2. Trung vị Median : - Giá trị nằm chính giữa dãy dữ liệu sau khi đã sắp xếp theo thứ tự. - Ít bị ảnh hưởng bởi giá trị ngoại lai hơn trung bình cộng, nên thường được dùng cho dữ liệu lệch như thu nhập, giá nhà hoặc tuổi thọ. 3. Yếu vị Mode : - Giá trị xuất hiện với tần suất cao nhất trong tập dữ liệu. - Có thể áp dụng cho cả dữ liệu định tính thang đo định danh . 4.2 Mức độ phân tán Measures of Dispersion Các đại lượng này đo lường mức độ trải rộng hay biến động của dữ liệu: 1. Khoảng biến thiên Range : MATH . 2. Phương sai Variance — MATH hoặc MATH : - Đo trung bình bình phương độ lệch của các quan sát so với trung bình cộng. - Công thức phương sai mẫu với hiệu chỉnh Bessel : MATH . 3. Độ lệch chuẩn Standard Deviation — MATH hoặc MATH : - Bằng căn bậc hai của phương sai: MATH . - Có cùng đơn vị đo với dữ liệu gốc nên dễ diễn giải trực tiếp hơn phương sai. 4. Tứ phân vị Quartiles và khoảng tứ phân vị IQR — Interquartile Range : - MATH phân vị 25% , MATH phân vị 50%, tức trung vị , MATH phân vị 75% . - MATH : bao phủ 50% dữ liệu ở vùng giữa và ít chịu ảnh hưởng của giá trị ngoại lai. 4.3 Tổng thể và mẫu Population vs. Sample - Tham số tổng thể Parameter : Đại lượng mô tả toàn bộ tổng thể, thường chưa biết và ký hiệu bằng chữ cái Hy Lạp MATH . - Thống kê mẫu Statistic : Đại lượng tính từ một mẫu quan sát được, ký hiệu bằng chữ cái Latinh MATH . - Lưu ý : Khi tính phương sai mẫu, ta chia cho MATH thay vì MATH để thu được ước lượng không chệch unbiased estimator cho phương sai tổng thể MATH . 5. Ví dụ minh họa Xét tập dữ liệu điểm thi của 5 sinh viên: MATH giả sử giá trị 100 là lỗi nhập liệu, tức một giá trị ngoại lai . - Mean : MATH , cao hơn nhiều so với mặt bằng chung của đa số sinh viên. - Median : Sắp xếp MATH , giá trị chính giữa là 8 , phản ánh sát thực tế hơn. 6. Triển khai trên Python python import numpy as np import pandas as pd from scipy import stats Tập dữ liệu có outlier data = np.array 5, 7, 8, 9, 100 print f"Dữ liệu: data " 1. Khuynh hướng tâm mean val = np.mean data median val = np.median data mode val = stats.mode data, keepdims=True .mode 0 print f"Mean: mean val " 25.8 print f"Median: median val " 8.0 print f"Mode: mode val " 2. Phân tán ddof=1 nghĩa là chia cho n-1 Sample Variance/Std var val = np.var data, ddof=1 std val = np.std data, ddof=1 iqr val = stats.iqr data print f"Sample Variance: var val:.2f " print f"Sample Std Dev: std val:.2f " print f"IQR: iqr val " 3. Sử dụng Pandas describe df = pd.DataFrame 'Score': data print "\n--- Pandas Describe ---" print df.describe 7. Giải thích và các lỗi thường gặp Ngộ nhận: "Trung bình cộng luôn tốt hơn trung vị" Trong phân phối đối xứng như phân phối chuẩn , trung bình cộng và trung vị trùng nhau. Tuy nhiên, với phân phối lệch như thu nhập , trung vị đại diện cho mức điển hình tốt hơn. Vì vậy, nên xem xét cả hai chỉ số cùng lúc. Lỗi: Quên đặt ddof=1 trong NumPy - numpy.std mặc định ddof=0 chia cho MATH , tương ứng độ lệch chuẩn tổng thể . - pandas.std mặc định ddof=1 chia cho MATH , tương ứng độ lệch chuẩn mẫu . - Khi tính trên dữ liệu mẫu bằng NumPy, cần truyền rõ tham số ddof=1 bậc tự do điều chỉnh . Giải thích: tự tay tính Mean, Median, SD và IQR trước và sau khi có 1 ngoại lai Hãy tự kiểm tra sức tàn phá của một điểm ngoại lai duy nhất trên mẫu lương của 5 nhân viên triệu đồng/tháng : 1. Mẫu gốc sạch, đối xứng : MATH . - Mean: MATH . - Median: phần tử đứng giữa thứ 3 MATH . - Độ lệch chuẩn mẫu chia MATH : MATH s = \sqrt \frac -3 ^2 + -1 ^2 + 0^2 + 2^2 + 2^2 4 = \sqrt \frac 18 4 = \sqrt 4.5 \approx 2.12. MATH - IQR: nửa dưới MATH ; nửa trên MATH . 2. Thay người thứ 5 bằng một giám đốc lương 115 triệu: MATH . - Mean: MATH tăng vọt +154% , cao hơn gấp đôi lương của cả 4 nhân viên đầu! . - Độ lệch chuẩn mẫu: MATH s \text mới = \sqrt \frac -23 ^2 + -21 ^2 + -20 ^2 + -18 ^2 + 82^2 4 = \sqrt \frac 8418 4 \approx 45.87 MATH tăng hơn 21 lần! . - Median mới: phần tử thứ 3 vẫn là MATH không nhúc nhích 1 xu! . - IQR mới: MATH với quy ước tính trên nửa dưới/nửa trên không gồm trung vị, hoặc đổi rất nhẹ tùy quy ước → độ phân tán lõi hầu như miễn nhiễm! Kết luận dễ nhớ: Khi gặp dữ liệu lệch phải thu nhập, thời gian phản hồi web, giá bất động sản , hãy luôn báo cáo Median + IQR song hành cùng Mean + SD .
