title: Bài 3: Trực Quan Hóa Dữ Liệu (Data Visualization)
content: Năm 1973, nhà thống kê Francis Anscombe công bố bốn bộ dữ liệu nhỏ mang tên Bộ tứ Anscombe khiến cả giới khoa học dữ liệu phải giật mình: cả bốn bộ đều có trung bình MATH bằng nhau 9.0 , trung bình MATH bằng nhau 7.5 , độ lệch chuẩn bằng nhau , hệ số tương quan giống hệt nhau MATH và đường hồi quy tuyến tính y hệt nhau MATH . Thế nhưng ngay khi vẽ lên mặt phẳng tọa độ, một bộ là đường thẳng nhiễu, một bộ là đường cong parabol hoàn hảo, một bộ là đường thẳng bị một điểm ngoại lai duy nhất kéo lệch, và bộ cuối cùng là một cột thẳng đứng cộng thêm một điểm lạc loài! Bài học bất hủ ấy khẳng định: đừng bao giờ tin các con số tóm tắt khi chưa nhìn thấy biểu đồ của dữ liệu . Trực quan hóa không phải khâu "trang trí cho slide đẹp mắt", mà là kính hiển vi đầu tiên giúp phát hiện cấu trúc ẩn, điểm ngoại lai và những cái bẫy thị giác. --- Kiến thức cần nhớ: Trực quan hóa dữ liệu trong thống kê nghiên cứu những gì? Chọn đúng biểu đồ là một quyết định toán học gắn liền với kiểu dữ liệu và câu hỏi phân tích, gồm bốn trụ cột : 1. Phân phối 1 biến Distribution : Histogram, KDE mật độ trơn và Boxplot — cho thấy đỉnh phân phối một đỉnh hay hai đỉnh? , độ lệch và các điểm ngoại lai theo quy tắc MATH . 2. Quan hệ giữa 2+ biến Relationships : Biểu đồ phân tán Scatter plot phát hiện quan hệ phi tuyến; biểu đồ đường Line chart cho chuỗi thời gian; Heatmap cho ma trận tương quan. 3. So sánh theo nhóm Comparison : Bar chart và Violin/Boxplot nhóm giúp đối chiếu nhanh phân phối giữa các phân khúc. 4. Độ trung thực thị giác Visual Integrity : Hiểu Hệ số nói dối Lie Factor của Edward Tufte để không bị đánh lừa bởi trục tung bị cắt ngang, biểu đồ 3D méo góc nhìn hay quy mô diện tích sai tỉ lệ. --- 1. Mục tiêu bài học Sau khi hoàn thành bài học này, người học có thể: - Hiểu vai trò của trực quan hóa dữ liệu trong quá trình khám phá dữ liệu Exploratory Data Analysis — EDA . - Vẽ và diễn giải các biểu đồ cơ bản: Histogram phân phối , Boxplot so sánh và phát hiện giá trị ngoại lai , Scatter plot mối quan hệ giữa hai biến . - Nhận diện các dạng biểu đồ gây hiểu lầm Misleading Graphs . - Sử dụng Matplotlib và Seaborn để tạo biểu đồ rõ ràng và đúng chuẩn trong Python. 2. Kiến thức tiền đề - Bài 1 và Bài 2 Các loại dữ liệu và Các đặc trưng số . - Thư viện matplotlib và seaborn . 3. Động lực và giới thiệu Các chỉ số tóm tắt như trung bình cộng hay phương sai cung cấp cái nhìn khái quát, nhưng đôi khi không thể hiện được cấu trúc thực sự của dữ liệu. Một ví dụ kinh điển là Bộ tứ Anscombe Anscombe's Quartet : bốn tập dữ liệu có cùng trung bình, phương sai và hệ số tương quan nhưng hình dạng phân bố hoàn toàn khác nhau. Trực quan hóa giúp ta quan sát trực tiếp hình dạng dữ liệu, phát hiện xu hướng, quy luật patterns và các điểm bất thường mà con số tóm tắt đơn lẻ dễ bỏ sót. 4. Các khái niệm cốt lõi và các loại biểu đồ cơ bản 4.1 Biểu đồ phân phối Distribution 1. Biểu đồ tần suất Histogram : - Chia miền giá trị của biến liên tục thành các khoảng bins và đếm số quan sát rơi vào mỗi khoảng. - Giúp nhận biết hình dạng phân phối: đối xứng hay lệch skewed , có một đỉnh hay nhiều đỉnh. 2. Ước lượng mật độ hạt nhân Kernel Density Estimation — KDE : - Làm trơn histogram để ước lượng đường cong hàm mật độ xác suất liên tục. 4.2 Biểu đồ so sánh và phát hiện ngoại lai 1. Biểu đồ hộp Boxplot : - Tóm tắt phân phối qua các mốc chính: giá trị nhỏ nhất trong phạm vi râu , MATH , trung vị Median , MATH và giá trị lớn nhất trong phạm vi râu . - Hữu ích để phát hiện giá trị ngoại lai outliers — các điểm nằm ngoài hai "râu" whiskers của hộp — và so sánh nhanh phân phối giữa các nhóm chẳng hạn thu nhập theo giới tính . 4.3 Biểu đồ mối quan hệ Relationship 1. Biểu đồ tán xạ Scatter Plot : - Biểu diễn đồng thời hai biến liên tục trên trục hoành X và trục tung Y . - Giúp quan sát chiều hướng và mức độ tương quan: tương quan dương cùng tăng , tương quan âm ngược chiều hoặc không có tương quan rõ rệt. 5. Ví dụ minh họa - Histogram : Biểu diễn phân phối chiều cao người trưởng thành thường có dạng hình chuông đối xứng phân phối chuẩn . - Scatter Plot : Biểu diễn giá nhà Y theo diện tích X thường cho thấy xu hướng đồng biến diện tích tăng thì giá tăng . 6. Triển khai trên Python Dưới đây là ví dụ minh họa ba loại biểu đồ trên tập dữ liệu giả lập gồm điểm hai môn Toán và Văn tương tự cách thực hành trên bộ dữ liệu kinh điển Iris . python import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns import numpy as np import pandas as pd Cài đặt style cho đẹp sns.set theme style="whitegrid" Tạo dữ liệu giả lập: Điểm thi 2 môn Toán và Văn np.random.seed 42 n students = 200 math scores = np.random.normal loc=7.0, scale=1.5, size=n students lit scores = 0.6 math scores + np.random.normal loc=2.0, scale=1.0, size=n students Giới hạn điểm trong 0, 10 math scores = np.clip math scores, 0, 10 lit scores = np.clip lit scores, 0, 10 df = pd.DataFrame 'Math': math scores, 'Literature': lit scores 1. Histogram & KDE Phân phối điểm Toán plt.figure figsize= 10, 5 sns.histplot data=df, x="Math", kde=True, bins=15, color="skyblue" plt.title "Phân phối điểm môn Toán" plt.xlabel "Điểm số" plt.ylabel "Số lượng sinh viên" plt.show 2. Boxplot So sánh điểm Toán và Văn plt.figure figsize= 8, 6 sns.boxplot data=df plt.title "So sánh phân phối điểm Toán và Văn" plt.ylabel "Điểm số" plt.show 3. Scatter Plot Tương quan Toán vs Văn plt.figure figsize= 8, 6 sns.scatterplot data=df, x="Math", y="Literature" plt.title "Mối quan hệ giữa điểm Toán và Văn" plt.show 7. Các lỗi thường gặp và biểu đồ gây hiểu lầm Misleading Graphs 1. Cắt trục tung trục Y không bắt đầu từ 0 : - Việc cắt bớt gốc 0 trên biểu đồ cột dễ phóng đại một chênh lệch nhỏ thành sự khác biệt lớn. Cần luôn kiểm tra phạm vi trục tung khi đọc biểu đồ. 2. Lạm dụng biểu đồ tròn Pie Chart : - Mắt người khó so sánh chính xác góc và diện tích, đặc biệt khi có nhiều nhóm có tỷ lệ gần nhau. Trong hầu hết trường hợp, biểu đồ cột Bar Chart truyền tải thông tin rõ ràng hơn. 3. Tương quan giả Spurious Correlations : - Hai đại lượng biến thiên cùng chiều trên biểu đồ không đồng nghĩa với quan hệ nhân quả Correlation MATH Causation . Ví dụ: doanh số bán kem và số vụ đuối nước cùng tăng vào mùa hè do cùng chịu tác động của biến ẩn là nhiệt độ. Giải thích: tự tay tính Hệ số nói dối Lie Factor khi biểu đồ cắt trục tung Bạn rất hay gặp những biểu đồ quảng cáo cho thấy doanh số hay hiệu năng "tăng vọt gấp ba lần", nhưng nhìn kỹ hóa ra chỉ tăng có 2%! Hãy dùng công thức Lie Factor của Edward Tufte để vạch trần trò ảo thuật thị giác đó bằng số cụ thể: MATH \text Lie Factor = \frac \text Mức thay đổi thể hiện trên hình vẽ \% \text Mức thay đổi thực tế của dữ liệu \% . MATH Giả sử tỷ lệ khách hàng hài lòng tăng từ 98% năm ngoái lên 100% năm nay: - Mức tăng thực tế của dữ liệu: MATH . - Biểu đồ trung thực trục tung bắt đầu từ MATH : Chiều cao hai cột là MATH và MATH → cột mới cao hơn đúng MATH → MATH hoàn toàn trung thực! . - Biểu đồ cắt trục tung trục tung bắt đầu từ MATH : - Chiều cao hiển thị của cột 1: MATH đơn vị. - Chiều cao hiển thị của cột 2: MATH đơn vị cao gấp 3 lần , tức tăng MATH trên hình vẽ! . - Tính Lie Factor : MATH \text Lie Factor = \frac 200\% 2.04\% \approx 98! MATH Chỉ bằng một thao tác cắt trục tung, biểu đồ đã phóng đại sự thật lên gần 100 lần ! Quy tắc thực hành: Với biểu đồ cột Bar chart mã hóa giá trị bằng độ dài cột , trục tung bắt buộc phải bắt đầu từ 0 . Chỉ biểu đồ đường — Line chart — mới được phép thu hẹp trục tung để soi xu hướng nhỏ, và phải ghi chú rõ phạm vi trục. Video tham khảo - StatQuest: Histograms, Clearly Explained https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBigTkBLU6g — StatQuest with Josh Starmer, tiếng Anh. Xem trước. Giải thích cách histogram phản ánh hình dạng phân phối, tương ứng biểu đồ đầu tiên trong ví dụ điểm Toán. - Boxplots are Awesome!!! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fHLhBnmwUM0 — StatQuest with Josh Starmer, tiếng Anh. Trình bày cách dùng boxplot để so sánh nhóm và nhận diện giá trị ngoại lai, khớp với ví dụ so sánh điểm Toán và Văn. - How to spot a misleading graph - Lea Gaslowitz https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E91bGT9BjYk — TED-Ed, tiếng Anh. Phân tích các cách cắt trục hoặc chọn tỷ lệ làm sai lệch thông điệp, liên quan trực tiếp đến mục biểu đồ gây hiểu lầm. 8. Bài tập 1. Python Tải tập dữ liệu Tips từ seaborn df = sns.load dataset 'tips' và thực hiện các yêu cầu sau: - Vẽ Histogram của cột total bill và nhận xét phân phối có bị lệch hay không. - Vẽ Boxplot của total bill phân nhóm theo day thứ trong tuần . Xác định ngày có mức chi tiêu cao nhất và kiểm tra xem có nhiều giá trị ngoại lai không. - Vẽ Scatter plot giữa total bill và tip để quan sát mối quan hệ giữa hai biến. - Nâng cao Thêm tham số hue="smoker" vào scatter plot để so sánh xu hướng tiền tip giữa nhóm có hút thuốc và không hút thuốc. 9. title: 02-04-00 Applications and recent developments
content: It is easy to skim Chapter 02—nominal vs. ordinal scales, mean vs. median, boxplots, Anscombe’s quartet—and assume it is just introductory warm-up before the “real” math starts. Then you step into a modern AI lab and discover that some of the biggest leaps in vision, language, and bioinformatics from 2021 to 2025 did not come from inventing a new neural architecture. They came from descriptive statistics at scale : filtering billions of noisy web pairs, catching corrupted class labels, and exposing misleading 2D visualizations! This optional note maps Chapter 02’s three foundational habits— what was measured , how it was summarized , and what the picture hid —onto four landmark data-centric systems: DataComp , Confident Learning cleanlab , t-SNE/UMAP distortion , and TabPFN . --- Key ideas: Why Descriptive Statistics Drives Data-Centric AI Three core statistical ideas sit beneath every modern data-curation pipeline. 1. Measurement Scales & Data Curation Nominal, Ordinal, Ratio Every column in a table carries a measurement scale that dictates which operations are meaningful averaging ZIP codes is nonsense; thresholding similarity scores is valid . Data-centric AI treats dataset filtering—deduplication, language tags, score histograms—as a primary scientific intervention rather than a throwaway preprocessing step. - Core questions: How much model accuracy comes from better data curation versus bigger architectures? - Real-world reach: Web-scale multimodal pretraining DataComp, DataComp-LM , medical registries, and tabular foundation models TabPFN . 2. Robust Location & Scale Estimators Breakdown Point The sample mean and standard deviation have a breakdown point of 0% —a single corrupted outlier can drag them to infinity! By contrast, the median has a 50% breakdown point and the interquartile range IQR has a 25% breakdown point . The exact same robustness logic extends to categorical labels when 3–10% of human annotations are wrong. - Core questions: Which summaries stay stable under sensor glitches or label noise? How can out-of-sample probabilities flag mislabeled rows? - Real-world reach: RobustScaler , cleanlab label auditing, financial outlier filtering, and industrial IoT pipelines. 3. Visual Statistics & Dimensionality-Reduction Distortion Just as Anscombe’s quartet proved that identical means, variances, and correlations can hide four radically different scatterplots, modern nonlinear embeddings t-SNE , UMAP are statistics that inevitably distort global distances when squashing 2,000 dimensions onto a flat 2D screen. - Core questions: Which geometric features local neighbors vs. global distances does a visualization preserve, and which does it fabricate? - Real-world reach: Single-cell genomics, LLM embedding explorers, and exploratory anomaly detection. --- Dataset design as descriptive statistics at scale Gadre, Ilharco, Fang, and colleagues DataComp , NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper files/paper/2023/hash/56332d41d55ad7ad8024aac625881be7-Abstract-Datasets and Benchmarks.html ; arXiv:2304.14108 https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14108 ; datacomp.ai https://www.datacomp.ai froze the training code of a CLIP model and varied only the training data . Starting from a 12.8-billion image–text pool CommonPool , they applied Chapter 02-style descriptive filters: English-language tags, CLIP similarity quantiles, deduplication, and aspect-ratio bounds. Their curated subset, DataComp-1B 1.4B pairs , trained a ViT-L/14 to 79.2% ImageNet zero-shot accuracy— +3.7 points ahead of OpenAI’s CLIP ViT-L/14 at matched compute! A language-model counterpart, DataComp-LM Li et al., NeurIPS 2024; arXiv:2406.11794 https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794 , confirmed the same rule for LLMs. When you inspect a histogram and trim junk rows in Pandas, you are running a miniature DataComp filter. Label errors and robust summaries A nominal class label is a measurement scale. If 5% of ImageNet tags are wrong, the sample mean of “accuracy” is a contaminated location estimate—the discrete cousin of a corrupted sensor reading. Northcutt, Jiang, and Chuang Confident Learning , JAIR 2021 https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.12125 estimate the joint distribution of noisy labels MATH and latent clean labels MATH from out-of-sample predicted probabilities, flagging likely mislabeled examples inside the open-source cleanlab https://docs.cleanlab.ai/ library. --- Worked Example 1: Mean/SD vs. Median/IQR Under One Corrupted Sensor Reading Suppose five temperature readings are cleanly recorded as MATH , and then a single glitch corrupts MATH , giving MATH . Compute both summaries by hand: | Summary Statistic | Clean data MATH | Corrupted data MATH | Shift | |-------------------|-----------------------------------|----------------------------------------|-------| | Mean MATH | MATH | MATH | +143% jump! | | Std. Dev. MATH population | MATH | MATH | 25× explosion! | | Median | MATH | MATH | 0% change! | | IQR MATH | MATH | MATH | 0% change! | One broken entry out of five completely destroys StandardScaler mean and SD , while RobustScaler median and IQR does not flinch! --- python import numpy as np from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, RobustScaler rng = np.random.default rng 0 x = rng.normal size= 200, 1 x 0 = 40.0 one broken sensor reading print "mean / sd:", StandardScaler .fit x .mean 0 , StandardScaler .fit x .scale 0 print "median / IQR-scale:", RobustScaler .fit x .center 0 , RobustScaler .fit x .scale 0 The printed mean jumps; the median barely moves. That is why data-centric papers talk about cleaning before fitting . --- Worked Example 2: Flagging a Label Error with Confident Learning by Hand Suppose a cat-vs-dog classifier produces out-of-sample predicted probabilities on 4 images labeled Cat MATH : - Image 1: MATH - Image 2: MATH - Image 3: MATH - Image 4: MATH How does Confident Learning decide whether Image 4 is actually a mislabeled Dog? 1. Compute the class confidence threshold MATH = average predicted MATH across all images labeled Dog suppose MATH . 2. Compare Image 4’s out-of-sample MATH ! 3. Because Image 4’s self-confidence for its given label MATH is tiny while its confidence for Dog clears the Dog threshold MATH , cleanlab places Image 4 into the off-diagonal cell MATH of the confident joint matrix and flags it for human review! --- Pictures that lie: embeddings as modern misleading graphs Anscombe’s quartet already showed four datasets with identical means, variances, and correlations yet four radically different shapes. The 2020s version is a 2D t-SNE or UMAP scatter plot of a 2,000-gene count matrix. Chari and Pachter PLOS Computational Biology , 2023; doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011288 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011288 proved mathematically and empirically that crushing thousands of dimensions into two necessarily warps global distances and cluster sizes—yet analysts routinely read distances between two UMAP islands as if they were real biological distances! The Chapter 02 moral survives intact: every plot is a statistic . Report what it preserves and what it distorts, and never run clustering directly on a 2D t-SNE/UMAP projection. Mixed types and a prior over tables Hollmann, Müller, Eggensperger, and Hutter TabPFN , ICLR 2023 https://iclr.cc/virtual/2023/poster/12113 ; arXiv:2207.01848 https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.01848 trained a Transformer once on synthetic tables drawn from a structural prior over mixed numeric/categorical features and causal graphs, allowing it to classify a brand-new small table in a single forward pass. The statistical takeaway is crystal clear: tabular modeling always begins by declaring which columns are nominal , ordinal , or ratio —ignoring measurement scales is not “end-to-end,” it is misspecified. --- Explanation: Four Habits of Data-Centric Statistical Hygiene Whenever you inherit a messy real-world dataset—whether 500 rows or 5 billion—run through these four checks slowly before touching a complex model. Step 1: Audit every column’s measurement scale first Separate nominal IDs/categories from ordered ranks and continuous ratios. Encoding a nominal category city id = 1, 2, 3 as a numeric integer silently injects fake arithmetic MATH into linear and distance-based models. Step 2: Check breakdown sensitivity before standardizing Compare mean vs. median and SD vs. IQR for every numeric feature. If the mean and median diverge sharply, a handful of outliers or heavy tails will distort ordinary standardization—switch to RobustScaler or a log transform log1p . Step 3: Audit the target labels with out-of-sample probabilities Never assume training labels are ground truth. Train a simple cross-validated baseline and inspect the top-20 rows with the largest loss or lowest predicted probability on their given label—you will often uncover systematic labeling bugs worth more than weeks of model tuning. Step 4: Treat 2D embeddings t-SNE / UMAP as exploratory sketches, not metric maps Use t-SNE/UMAP to spot local clusters or data glitches, then verify every hypothesis back in the original feature space using actual distances, gene expression levels, or summary statistics before drawing scientific conclusions. --- What to carry forward When a paper says “we filtered Common Crawl by CLIP score,” “we used cleanlab on the labels,” or “do not cluster on the UMAP,” it is speaking Chapter 02. Later probability chapters add sampling models; they do not replace the discipline of type, summary, and picture. title: 03-02-00 Applications and recent developments
content: A weather app says “80% chance of rain,” and you expect it to rain on roughly four out of five days with that forecast. Now ask a modern deep neural network whether a tumor scan is malignant, and it prints 0.99 —yet when you check all scans where it printed 0.99 , only 82% were actually malignant! Something broke between the number coming out of softmax and the real conditional probability MATH . Sample spaces, conditional probability, Bayes’ theorem, and independence are not dusty textbook exercises. They are the exact mathematical tools production AI systems misuse whenever they mistake a raw softmax score for a frequency, a next-token likelihood for a factual belief, or an observational conditional MATH for a causal effect MATH . This optional note traces four live battlegrounds of Chapter 03 probability in modern computer science 2021–2023 . --- Key ideas: Where Does Chapter 03 Probability Live in Modern AI? Three probability concepts sit directly behind calibration, LLMs, spam filters, and causal inference. 1. Conditional Probability & Calibration Frequency Matching A probabilistic classifier outputs a score MATH . Calibration demands that conditional on the model’s own forecast MATH , the true empirical frequency of positive outcomes actually equals MATH . Expected Calibration Error ECE measures the average gap between confidence and reality across probability bins. - Core questions: Is an AI model overconfident? Can post-hoc temperature scaling or Platt scaling repair its reliability without hurting accuracy? - Real-world reach: Medical diagnosis triage, autonomous driving risk thresholds, credit-default pricing, and weather forecasting. 2. Bayes’ Rule, Likelihoods & Conditional Independence Bayes’ theorem links prior beliefs MATH and generative likelihoods MATH to the posterior MATH . Assuming conditional independence yields Naive Bayes still widely deployed for text classification , while autoregressive LLMs factorize joint sequence probabilities via the chain rule MATH , MATH , often restores calibration without changing a single top-1 prediction! Minderer et al. NeurIPS 2021 ; arXiv:2106.07998 https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.07998 added an architectural twist: modern Vision Transformers are often better calibrated out of the box than older CNNs. In tabular ML, scikit-learn’s CalibratedClassifierCV https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html Platt scaling or isotonic regression performs the same repair. --- Worked Example 1: Computing ECE and Temperature Scaling by Hand Suppose a binary classifier evaluates MATH patients across two confidence bins: - Bin 1 60 patients, avg predicted probability MATH : only 48 are positive MATH . - Bin 2 40 patients, avg predicted probability MATH : 26 are positive MATH . 1. Compute Expected Calibration Error ECE : MATH 2. Apply Temperature Scaling MATH to an overconfident logit vector MATH : - Before scaling MATH : MATH . - After scaling MATH : MATH . Notice the predicted class Class 1 did not change at all , yet the overconfident 88.1% softened cleanly down to 73.1%! --- What an LLM means by “probability” A language model defines a conditional distribution on the next token, MATH , built from the chain rule over a vast discrete vocabulary. After RLHF fine-tuning, however, raw token probabilities become sharply overconfident. Tian, Mitchell, Zhou, Sharma, Rafailov, Yao, Finn, and Manning Just Ask for Calibration , EMNLP 2023 https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.330/ showed that verbalized confidences “I am 70% sure” from ChatGPT / GPT-4 / Claude often cut ECE roughly in half compared to token log-probabilities on TriviaQA, SciQ, and TruthfulQA. The Chapter 03 distinction is razor-sharp: MATH is a linguistic likelihood , whereas MATH is the epistemic posterior you actually wanted. Naive Bayes that still ships The spam-filter calculation in Chapter 03 is not a classroom toy. scikit-learn’s MultinomialNB https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/naive bayes.html still filters mail and tags documents in production because, under conditional independence , MATH P x 1,\ldots,x d\mid y = \prod j=1 ^d P x j\mid y , MATH training reduces to counting word frequencies and prediction reduces to summing log-ratios. Production engineers know words are not independent given the class—so Naive Bayes probabilities are often pushed near 0 or 1 poorly calibrated! , yet the decision boundary remains remarkably fast and accurate. Light causal graphs: MATH is not MATH Simpson’s paradox is the classic proof that conditioning on an observational group is not the same as intervening. Sharma and Kiciman DoWhy , arXiv:2011.04216 https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.04216 ; pywhy.org/dowhy https://www.pywhy.org/dowhy/ turn this into a four-step software workflow: Model a causal graph, Identify whether MATH can be computed from observational conditionals, Estimate it, and Refute it with placebo/confounder stress tests. --- Worked Example 2: Simpson’s Paradox by Hand — Why MATH A hospital records recovery rates MATH for a new drug MATH versus standard care MATH , split by initial patient severity MATH : | Patient Severity MATH | New Drug MATH Recovery | Standard Care MATH Recovery | Winner inside subgroup | |------------------------|-------------------------------|------------------------------------|------------------------| | Mild MATH | MATH | MATH | New Drug +10% | | Severe MATH | MATH | MATH | New Drug +10% | | Pooled Total | MATH | MATH | Standard Care +14%! | Look at that jaw-dropping reversal! - Observational conditional: MATH . Naive Bayes-table reading says the new drug is harmful! - Why it flipped: Doctors gave the new drug mostly to Severe patients 400 vs. 100 , so severity MATH confounded treatment MATH ! - Backdoor interventional formula with MATH and MATH : MATH MATH Giving the new drug actually raises recovery by +10 percentage points ! Conditioning MATH vs. MATH answered the wrong question; causal adjustment MATH vs. MATH answered the policy question. --- Explanation: Four Probability Questions to Ask Any AI System Before trusting a number printed between 0.00 and 1.00 by a modern ML or LLM system, walk through these four Chapter 03 questions slowly. Step 1: Is this number a calibrated frequency or just a ranking score? Check a reliability diagram or ECE on a held-out set. A model with 0.95 AUC can still be wildly overconfident ECE = 0.15 until you apply temperature scaling or isotonic calibration. Step 2: What exact event is inside MATH ? For an LLM, MATH measures how likely human text continues with the word “Paris,” not necessarily MATH . Never confuse a generative likelihood with a truth posterior. Step 3: Which conditional independence assumptions were silently baked in? Naive Bayes assumes features are independent given the label; many RAG/retrieval pipelines assume chunks are independent. Violating independence may leave top-1 classification intact while severely distorting predicted probabilities. Step 4: Are we predicting observational or deciding interventional ? If you only want to predict who will default or recover under existing policies, MATH is right. The moment you plan to change a policy, assign a drug, or offer a discount, you need MATH —either via a randomized A/B test or an explicit causal graph. --- What to carry forward When a paper says “we report ECE,” “we asked the model for a verbal probability,” “we shipped MultinomialNB,” or “we identified the effect in DoWhy,” it is speaking Chapter 03. Random-variable lessons come next; they refine how we number events, not the meaning of MATH . title: 04-05-00 Applications and recent developments
content: Open a warehouse inventory dashboard at Amazon, a cloud-server latency monitor, or a frontier discrete diffusion model for text, and you might expect to find exotic mathematics completely divorced from undergraduate probability. Look under the hood, and you will find the exact named random variables from Chapter 04— Bernoulli , Poisson , Negative Binomial , Categorical , and Gaussian —acting as the probabilistic “output heads” of modern deep learning systems! Neural networks do not replace probability distributions; they simply learn rich mappings from raw context into the parameters MATH of those exact families. This optional note does not re-derive PMFs. Instead, it shows how three Chapter 04 families power modern 2020–2024 systems: overdispersed count forecasting DeepAR , continuous-time event arrivals Poisson & Neural Hawkes processes , and discrete diffusion generative models SEDD . --- Key ideas: Where Do Named Distributions Power Modern Systems? Three pillars connect Chapter 04 random variables directly to production forecasting and generative AI. 1. Discrete Count Families & Overdispersion Poisson vs. Negative Binomial A Poisson variable enforces the rigid identity MATH . Real-world retail orders, ad clicks, and support tickets are almost always overdispersed MATH : quiet days alternate with viral spikes. Adding a Gamma-distributed random rate turns Poisson into the Negative Binomial family, allowing mean and variance to decouple cleanly. - Core questions: Why does a Gaussian loss fail on sparse nonnegative counts? How do we predict a full probability distribution of demand rather than a single average? - Real-world reach: Retail inventory optimization DeepAR , insurance claim frequency, and hospital ER admission forecasting. 2. Temporal Point Processes Poisson & Hawkes Processes A Poisson process extends the Poisson random variable into continuous time: arrivals in disjoint windows are independent and memoryless. When one event triggers a cascade of follow-up events earthquakes and aftershocks, viral tweets, high-frequency trades , the arrival rate MATH becomes history-dependent—yielding Hawkes and Neural Temporal Point Processes . - Core questions: How do we model the exact timestamps MATH . The Negative Binomial distribution keeps a mean MATH while adding a dispersion parameter MATH so that MATH . In production, scikit-learn’s PoissonRegressor https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear model.PoissonRegressor.html and TweedieRegressor provide linear count models, while Salinas, Flunkert, Gasthaus, and Januschowski DeepAR , International Journal of Forecasting 36, 2020 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2019.07.001 ; arXiv:1704.04110 https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.04110 attach a Negative Binomial or Gaussian likelihood head to a shared recurrent neural network so thousands of retail products borrow statistical strength from each other. The output is not a single point guess—it is a full predictive PMF you can sample to set safety-stock quantiles. --- Worked Example 1: Poisson vs. Negative Binomial on Bursty Retail Demand Suppose an online store averages MATH orders per day for a jacket. Compare what a Poisson model versus a Negative Binomial model with dispersion MATH predicts about daily variability: 1. Poisson MATH : - Mean MATH , Variance MATH , Standard deviation MATH . - Rough “mean + 2 SD” safety-stock threshold: MATH jackets. 2. Negative Binomial MATH : - Mean MATH , Variance MATH , Standard deviation MATH . - Rough “mean + 2 SD” safety-stock threshold: MATH jackets! Why this matters: Both distributions share the exact same average demand 4 jackets/day , yet the Poisson model underestimates daily volatility by over 40%—causing frequent stockouts during sudden spikes! Choosing the right Chapter 04 likelihood head directly translates into real warehouse revenue. --- python import numpy as np from sklearn.linear model import PoissonRegressor rng = np.random.default rng 0 x = rng.normal size= 400, 2 lam = np.exp 0.4 x :, 0 - 0.2 x :, 1 y = rng.poisson lam model = PoissonRegressor alpha=1e-4 .fit x, y print "mean predicted λ:", model.predict x .mean , "mean y:", y.mean If the printed means disagree badly, the log-link Poisson is the wrong family—not “the neural net failed.” Poisson processes in systems A Poisson random variable counts events in a fixed window. A Poisson process lets that window slide: increments on disjoint intervals are independent, and the count on an interval of length MATH is MATH . Request arrivals, crash dumps, and trades are routinely modeled this way before anyone mentions a neural net. When past events excite the future a popular post triggers more posts , the intensity MATH becomes history-dependent: a Hawkes process , and then a neural temporal point process . Mei and Eisner The Neural Hawkes Process , NeurIPS 2017 https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2017/hash/6463c88460bd63bbe256e495c63aa40b-Abstract.html replace the additive kernel with a continuous-time LSTM, and Shchur, Türkmen, Januschowski, and Günnemann IJCAI 2021 ; arXiv:2104.03528 https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.03528 survey modern transformer and intensity-free point processes. --- Worked Example 2: Memoryless Poisson Arrivals vs. a Self-Exciting Hawkes Spike Suppose an API server receives requests at baseline rate MATH requests/second. 1. Homogeneous Poisson Process over a MATH -second window: - Total expected arrivals: MATH . - Probability of zero requests in 2 seconds: MATH 0.25% . - Memorylessness: even if 5 requests arrived in the previous second, the rate for the next second stays frozen at MATH req/s. 2. Hawkes Process MATH with jump MATH and decay MATH : - The instant a request arrives at MATH , the intensity jumps from MATH to MATH req/s! - After MATH quiet second, the excitement decays exponentially to MATH req/s. - This exact self-exciting term explains why server crashes and viral retweets arrive in bursts rather than smooth Poisson intervals! --- Discrete generative models as PMFs An autoregressive language model is a huge categorical random variable at each site: MATH . Diffusion models that conquered images relied on a continuous Gaussian score MATH , which does not exist on discrete tokens. Lou, Meng, and Ermon Discrete Diffusion Modeling by Estimating the Ratios of the Data Distribution , ICML 2024 https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/lou24a.html ; arXiv:2310.16834 https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.16834 ; code Score-Entropy-Discrete-Diffusion https://github.com/louaaron/Score-Entropy-Discrete-Diffusion define a score entropy that matches discrete probability ratios MATH to build SEDD —competitive with GPT-2-scale autoregressive models while supporting flexible infilling. Austin et al.’s D3PM NeurIPS 2021 https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2021/hash/958c530554f2820e0d14e14d964d48d9-Abstract.html is the earlier discrete-diffusion formulation still cited beside SEDD. The sampling-distribution lesson then explains why a Monte Carlo estimate of perplexity or coverage needs a stated MATH : you are looking at MATH , not at one lucky generation. --- Explanation: How a Neural Network Outputs a Probability Distribution Students often ask: “How does a deep learning model like DeepAR or SEDD connect to Chapter 04 PMFs?” Follow these four steps slowly. Step 1: Separate the feature extractor from the probability family A neural network RNN, Transformer, MLP takes messy inputs history, text, context and produces a hidden vector MATH . By itself, MATH has no probabilistic meaning until you map it to the parameters of a chosen distribution. Step 2: Enforce parameter constraints with activation functions Count rates MATH must be strictly positive MATH or MATH ; categorical probabilities MATH must be nonnegative and sum to 1 MATH ; Gaussian standard deviations MATH must be positive. Step 3: Train by minimizing the negative log-PMF Maximum Likelihood Instead of squared error MATH which secretly assumes a constant-variance Gaussian! , you plug the observed count or token directly into MATH and backpropagate. Step 4: Sample from the output distribution at decision time Once trained, you don’t just read the mean! You draw 1,000 Monte Carlo trajectories from the Negative Binomial or Categorical head to compute 95% inventory quantiles, tail crash probabilities, or diverse text generations. --- What to carry forward When a paper says “negative-binomial likelihood,” “neural Hawkes intensity,” or “score entropy on tokens,” it is speaking Chapter 04. Estimation and tests come later; they act on these same named families. title: 05-03-00 Optional: Estimation in Modern Machine Learning
content: Suppose a brand-new backpack launches on an e-commerce site, receives 2 impressions, and 1 shopper clicks it—giving a raw click-through rate of MATH . Meanwhile, a bestselling backpack with 10,000 impressions has 1,800 clicks MATH . If you rank products by raw Maximum Likelihood MATH , every lucky 1-for-2 rookie shoots straight to the top of page one while proven bestsellers sink! This optional lesson does not replace the point- and interval-estimation theory in Chapter 05. It reveals how those exact estimators run the engines of modern AI and data science: Maximum Likelihood inside deep networks and LLMs, Method of Moments for multimodal mixtures, Empirical Bayes shrinkage inside production search ranking, and Bootstrap / Conformal intervals when analytic standard errors vanish. After working through it you should be able to recognize cross-entropy training as maximum likelihood, explain why moment matching is still used for Gaussian mixtures, compute and implement a Beta–Binomial empirical-Bayes shrinker, and contrast a bootstrap interval with a conformal prediction set. The prerequisites are the required lessons on point estimation bias, variance, MLE, method of moments and interval estimation confidence intervals and the bootstrap , plus elementary Python with NumPy. --- Key ideas: How Chapter 05 Estimators Scale to Modern ML Four classical estimation pillars map directly onto 2022–2026 production ML systems. 1. Maximum Likelihood Estimation MLE as Deep Learning Loss Minimizing cross-entropy in image classification or next-token loss in an LLM is literally maximizing the log-likelihood MATH . Scaling laws like Chinchilla are empirical tradeoffs between parameter dimension MATH and sample size MATH for that exact likelihood. - Core questions: When does penalized MLE work well despite non-convexity and over-parameterization? - Real-world reach: LLM pretraining, computer vision classifiers, and probabilistic forecasting. 2. Method of Moments MoM & Tensor Decomposition When a likelihood surface has many local traps like Gaussian Mixture Models , EM can stall in a poor local optimum. Method of Moments equates empirical moments means, covariances, third-order tensors to theoretical moments—providing globally consistent estimators and smart initializers for EM. - Core questions: How can implicit moment tensors avoid MATH memory blow-up in high dimensions? - Real-world reach: Speaker recognition, single-cell clustering, topic modeling, and anomaly detection. 3. Empirical Bayes & James–Stein Shrinkage When estimating thousands of parallel rates product CTRs, hospital mortality rates, baseball batting averages with wildly unequal sample sizes MATH , Empirical Bayes estimates a shared prior from the whole panel and shrinks noisy small- MATH estimates toward that prior—drastically lowering total MSE. - Core questions: How much weight should we give the population prior versus an item’s own clicks? - Real-world reach: Amazon/e-commerce cold-start ranking, ad-click prediction, and genomics differential expression. --- Why estimation left the textbook A ranking service, a language model, and a clustering pipeline all solve the same formal problem you have already studied: given a sample MATH , produce MATH and, when a decision is costly, an uncertainty interval around it. What changed between 2022 and 2026 is not the definition of an estimator—it is the scale, latency, cold-start sparsity, and compute budget that dictate which estimator wins. Maximum likelihood is how modern networks learn For i.i.d. observations the MLE maximizes MATH In a classifier, MATH is a softmax, and the average negative log-likelihood is identically the cross-entropy loss used in PyTorch and TensorFlow. Training with SGD is computational MLE: the score function MATH is backpropagated rather than set to zero in closed form. Autoregressive language models make the same identification token by token, maximizing MATH \sum t \log p \theta w t \mid w s = m 1-m /v - 1 s = m 1 - m / max v, eps - 1 s = max s, 1.0 return s m, s 1 - m def posterior ctr clicks, imps, alpha, beta : """Empirical-Bayes posterior mean CTR.""" return alpha + clicks / alpha + beta + imps Intervals when the analytic standard error is missing The required interval-estimation lesson constructs MATH and bootstrap percentile intervals. Deep networks with millions of weights break Hessian-based standard errors. Two modern tools fill the gap: - Bootstrap / Deep Ensembles: resample training data or random seeds and read empirical percentiles. - Split Conformal Prediction Angelopoulos & Bates, 2023 : use a held-out calibration fold to produce a finite-sample prediction set MATH satisfying MATH under exchangeability alone—a prediction interval for MATH , not a confidence interval for MATH . python import numpy as np def split conformal interval calib scores, q=0.9 : """ Split-conformal quantile for absolute residuals. Args: calib scores: |y - f x | on a held-out calibration fold q: target coverage, e.g. 0.9 Returns: Residual half-width to add/subtract from f x new """ n = len calib scores level = np.ceil n + 1 q / n return np.quantile calib scores, min level, 1.0 , method="higher" --- Explanation: Matching the Estimator to the Problem’s Geometry How does a senior statistician decide between MLE, Method of Moments, Empirical Bayes, and Conformal Prediction on a real project? Follow these four steps slowly. Step 1: Check whether the likelihood is clean and well-identified If your data follow a smooth exponential family logistic, Poisson, Gaussian and optimization converges reliably, MLE or penalized MLE achieves the lowest asymptotic variance Cramér–Rao bound . Step 2: Check for multimodal likelihood traps In latent-variable models mixtures, topic models, HMMs , pure likelihood optimization gets stuck in local peaks. Use Method of Moments to find a consistent global starting point, then refine with EM. Step 3: Check whether you are estimating thousands of sparse units simultaneously Whenever you have a panel of many items/users/stores with tiny sample sizes MATH , raw per-unit MLE has catastrophic variance. Empirical Bayes borrows strength across the whole panel via a data-estimated prior—trading tiny bias for massive variance reduction. Step 4: Ask whether you need a parameter CI or a future-outcome prediction interval If you want uncertainty around an average treatment effect MATH , use a confidence interval or bootstrap. If you want a guarantee that a specific customer’s future outcome MATH falls inside your interval, use conformal prediction on a clean calibration split. --- What a data scientist should take away Choose the estimator that matches the structure of the problem, not the prestige of the model class. If the observation model is a well-specified exponential family and you can optimize it, use MLE or a regularized version . If the likelihood is multimodal or you need a theoretically identified initializer, match moments. If you have a large panel of sparse units, shrink with an empirical-Bayes prior. If you need a finite-sample coverage guarantee around a black-box prediction, prefer conformal or the bootstrap to a naive normal interval. Challenges and extensions MLE in deep nets is computationally successful and inferentially delicate: standard errors, model misspecification, and train–serve skew all break textbook asymptotics. Method-of-moments estimators can have large finite-sample variance even when consistent; implicit tensors reduce cost, not statistical noise. Empirical Bayes assumes exchangeability across items; a sudden assortment shift silently mis-estimates MATH . Conformal coverage is marginal, not conditional on a rare slice of users. Open directions that sit on top of this chapter include likelihood-free estimation simulation-based inference, score matching , hierarchical empirical Bayes for many related ranking markets, and conformal methods under distribution shift. content: Imagine a product manager watching a live A/B test dashboard every morning over coffee. On Day 1, MATH . On Day 2, MATH . On Day 4, the dashboard flashes green: MATH ! Thrilled, the team stops the test and ships the new checkout button—never realizing that by peeking 20 times and stopping at the first green flash, they quietly inflated their false-positive rate from 5% to nearly 25% ! This optional lesson leaves the definitions of MATH , MATH -values, and Type I/II errors untouched and follows them straight into the massive engines that run them tens of thousands of times a day: industrial A/B platforms , sequential anytime-valid testing e-values / mSPRT , genome-wide association studies Bonferroni , and False Discovery Rate Benjamini–Hochberg & online FDR . You should finish able to compute a two-proportion MATH -test and Sample Ratio Mismatch check by hand, explain why peeking breaks fixed-sample MATH -values, run Benjamini–Hochberg versus Bonferroni by hand, and sketch how always-valid MATH -values restore rigor. --- Key ideas: How Hypothesis Testing Scales Up Three statistical ideas govern testing when you move from one textbook experiment to 10,000 live experiments. 1. Industrial A/B Testing & Data Integrity SRM Every online A/B test is a two-sample hypothesis test MATH backed by strict randomization hygiene. Before trusting any lift, platforms run a Sample Ratio Mismatch SRM MATH goodness-of-fit test checking whether the observed user split matches the intended 50/50 allocation—catching logging bugs and bot traffic before bad decisions ship. - Core questions: Is the observed lift statistically significant, practically meaningful, and free of assignment bugs? - Real-world reach: Product experimentation at Microsoft, Google, Meta, Netflix, and e-commerce platforms. 2. Sequential Testing & Anytime-Valid Inference e-Values & Martingales Classical MATH -values assume a single pre-committed sample size MATH . Safe anytime-valid inference mSPRT, e-values , test martingales MATH uses Ville’s inequality MATH so you can monitor continuously and stop whenever you want without ever breaking the MATH false-positive guarantee. - Core questions: How much extra sample size does continuous monitoring cost in exchange for peeking safety? - Real-world reach: Commercial A/B platforms Optimizely, Statsig , adaptive clinical trials, and continuous safety monitoring. 3. Multiplicity Control FWER vs. FDR vs. Online FDR Testing MATH independent true nulls at MATH gives a MATH chance of at least one false alarm MATH at MATH ! . Bonferroni controls the Family-Wise Error Rate FWER zero false alarms—vital in GWAS genetics , while Benjamini–Hochberg controls the False Discovery Rate FDR expected share of false alarms among discoveries—vital in dashboards and genomics . Online FDR extends this to endless streams of experiments. - Core questions: When do we pay for strict FWER versus more powerful FDR control? - Real-world reach: Genome-wide association studies GWAS , RNA-seq differential expression, and ad-ranking metric scorecards. --- A/B testing is hypothesis testing with a product manager attached An online controlled experiment tests conversion probabilities MATH control and MATH treatment : MATH with a two-sample MATH -test for proportions or a MATH -test for continuous metrics. Kohavi, Tang, and Xu 2020 document platforms running tens of thousands of tests a year, while Kohavi, Deng, and Vermeer 2022 catalog common intuition busters treating a 95% CI as a 95% probability for the current run, misusing post-hoc power, or trimming outliers after seeing the result . --- Worked Example 1: Two-Proportion MATH -Test & Sample Ratio Mismatch Check by Hand Suppose a 50/50 checkout A/B test observes: - Control: MATH conversions out of MATH users MATH . - Treatment: MATH conversions out of MATH users MATH , a MATH percentage-point lift . 1. Compute the two-proportion MATH -test: - Pooled rate: MATH . - Standard error: MATH . - Test statistic: MATH . At MATH , we do not reject MATH yet—the 2.5% lift is not distinguishable from sampling noise at MATH per arm! 2. Now run a Sample Ratio Mismatch SRM check on a second 50/50 experiment that logged MATH and MATH users total MATH , expected MATH each : MATH Even though 48.5% vs. 51.5% looks “close enough” to the naked eye, MATH screams that a redirect bug or bot filter broke randomization—invalidating every downstream metric! --- python import numpy as np from scipy import stats def two proportion ztest success c, n c, success t, n t : """ Two-sided z-test for H0: p T = p C. Returns: z, p value, p c, p t, lift """ p c = success c / n c p t = success t / n t p pool = success c + success t / n c + n t se = np.sqrt p pool 1 - p pool 1 / n c + 1 / n t z = p t - p c / se p value = 2 stats.norm.sf abs z return z, p value, p c, p t, p t - p c Peeking, optional stopping, and sequential tests A fixed-sample MATH -value is valid at one pre-chosen MATH . Refreshing a dashboard daily and stopping at the first MATH inflates Type I error dramatically. Johari, Koomen, Pekelis, and Walsh 2022 formalize always-valid MATH -values satisfying MATH for every data-dependent stopping time MATH using a mixture sequential probability ratio test mSPRT . Ramdas, Grünwald, Vovk, and Shafer 2023 unify this inside safe anytime-valid inference using e-values / test martingales MATH with MATH : by Ville’s inequality , MATH so MATH stays valid at every single refresh! The price is statistical power: always-valid tests require slightly wider rejection boundaries and thus larger average MATH than fixed-horizon tests. python import numpy as np def peeking inflation n looks=20, n per look=200, p=0.1, n sims=4000, alpha=0.05 : """ Type I error if you stop at the first p < alpha under a true null. """ rng = np.random.default rng 0 false reject = 0 for in range n sims : c = t = 0 nc = nt = 0 rejected = False for look in range n looks : c += rng.binomial n per look, p t += rng.binomial n per look, p nc += n per look nt += n per look , pval, = two proportion ztest c, nc, t, nt if pval < alpha: rejected = True break false reject += rejected return false reject / n sims Running that function with the defaults yields a Type I error near 20–25% , not 5%—which is why sequential methodology moved straight from clinical trials into consumer software. Multiple testing: genomes, ads, and online FDR Test MATH independent true nulls at level MATH and the chance of at least one false positive explodes to MATH . Two corrections anchor practice: - Family-wise error Bonferroni : reject at MATH . In GWAS Uffelmann et al., 2021 , ~1 million independent genomic variants yield the iconic threshold MATH —prioritizing reproducibility over power. - False Discovery Rate Benjamini–Hochberg, 1995 : controls MATH . Sort MATH , find the largest MATH satisfying MATH , and reject MATH . - Online FDR Robertson, Wason, & Ramdas, 2023 : procedures like LORD and SAFFRON manage an MATH -wealth budget across endless streams of arriving experiments. --- Worked Example 2: Bonferroni vs. Benjamini–Hochberg by Hand MATH Metrics Suppose an A/B scorecard tests MATH product metrics at target level MATH , returning sorted MATH -values: MATH Compare all three decision rules side by side: | Rank MATH | MATH | Unadjusted MATH | Bonferroni MATH | BH Threshold MATH | MATH ? | |------------|-------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|------------------------------------|----------------------------| | 1 | MATH | Reject | Reject | MATH | Yes ✓ | | 2 | MATH | Reject | Keep | MATH | Yes ✓ | | 3 | MATH | Reject | Keep | MATH | Yes ✓ largest MATH | | 4 | MATH | Reject | Keep | MATH | No ✗ | | 5 | MATH | Keep | Keep | MATH | No ✗ | - Unadjusted: rejects 4 metrics inflated false-positive risk! . - Bonferroni FWER : rejects only 1 metric MATH —ultra-conservative. - Benjamini–Hochberg FDR : rejects 3 metrics ranks 1, 2, and 3 , keeping the expected proportion of false discoveries among those 3 below 5%! --- python import numpy as np def benjamini hochberg p values, alpha=0.05 : """ BH rejection mask. Returns a boolean array aligned with p values. """ p = np.asarray p values m = len p order = np.argsort p thresh = alpha np.arange 1, m + 1 / m below = p order <= thresh if not below.any : return np.zeros m, dtype=bool cutoff = np.max np.where below 0 rejected = np.zeros m, dtype=bool rejected order : cutoff + 1 = True return rejected Inference for many coefficients is the same problem In a ranking or ads regression with thousands of features, celebrating every coefficient with MATH is a classic multiple-testing trap. Production teams either treat coefficients purely as predictive weights, apply BH/knockoffs for controlled variable selection, or regularize and evaluate out-of-sample. --- Explanation: Why Peeking and Multiple Testing Are the Exact Same Trap At first glance, peeking at one A/B test 20 times and testing 20 different metrics once look like different problems. Walk through these four steps to see why they are mathematically twins. Step 1: Under MATH , a MATH -value is a uniform random draw on MATH On a single pre-registered look at a single metric, MATH . Step 2: Taking the minimum over many looks or metrics shifts the distribution left Whether you take MATH across time OR MATH across columns, you are asking for the extreme minimum of 20 random draws—which drops below MATH far more than 5% of the time! Step 3: Why e-values and martingales defeat peeking cleanly Think of an e-value MATH as a gambler’s wealth starting at MATH dollar playing a fair game against MATH . Because MATH , no stopping strategy—not even peeking every millisecond—can give a gambler more than a 5% chance of ever multiplying MATH 20 MATH ! Step 4: Match the guardrails to the real business cost Use SRM first to verify clean data; use always-valid MATH -values or fixed pre-committed horizons to stop peeking; use Bonferroni when a single false alarm is catastrophic GWAS, safety ; and use Benjamini–Hochberg when screening dozens of exploratory segments or metrics. --- Challenges and extensions Peeking is not the only validity threat. Interference one user’s treatment changes another user’s outcome , novelty effects, and Sample Ratio Mismatch all produce significant results that are not treatment effects. Always-valid tests buy validity with sample size; teams that cannot wait sometimes prefer a hard cap on looks group sequential designs instead of a fully sequential e-process. Online FDR needs a well-defined stream; quietly dropping failed tests from the stream breaks the proof. Extensions that sit on this chapter include variance-reduced tests CUPED, taken up in Chapter 07 , causal inference when assignment is not a clean Bernoulli, and e-value aggregation for living meta-analysis. content: Run an ordinary A/B test on weekly user revenue, and you immediately hit a wall: a few “whale” shoppers spend MATH 0, so your standard error is enormous—meaning you would need to wait eight weeks to detect a real 1% lift! Yet you already know how much each user spent last week, before the experiment even started. Subtracting out that predictable pre-experiment baseline cuts your variance in half—letting you finish the exact same experiment in four weeks instead of eight , for free! This optional lesson takes Chapter 07’s linear regression tools straight into the four workhorses that modern industry and causal machine learning actually ship: Generalized Linear Models GLMs for non-Gaussian outcomes, Mixed-Effects Models for repeated user sessions, CUPED / Lin regression adjustment for randomized experiments, and Double/Debiased Machine Learning DML when treatment is observational rather than randomized. --- Key ideas: Four Extensions of Linear Regression Every tool in this lesson relaxes one specific assumption of classical OLS MATH . 1. Generalized Linear Models GLMs — Relaxing Gaussian Noise Classical OLS lets predictions go negative and assumes constant variance. GLMs keep the clean linear predictor MATH while plugging in a link function MATH and an exponential-family likelihood Bernoulli/logit, Poisson/log, Tweedie . - Core questions: How do we get calibrated, auditable models for counts, probabilities, and zero-inflated insurance claims? - Real-world reach: Wide & Deep ad click models, actuarial insurance pricing, and epidemiology rate modeling. 2. Linear Mixed-Effects Models LMM / GLMM — Relaxing i.i.d. Rows When the same user logs 30 sessions, treating all 30 rows as independent OLS observations artificially inflates your sample size and shrinks standard errors—manufacturing fake significance. Mixed models add a random intercept MATH per user/cluster to capture within-user correlation honestly. - Core questions: How much variance lives between users versus within users? - Real-world reach: Longitudinal clinical trials, neuroscience recordings, and session-level product logs. 3. Variance Reduction CUPED & Causal Machine Learning Double ML In randomized experiments, regression isn’t needed for causal identification—it is used purely to crush noise variance CUPED , Lin’s interacted OLS . In observational data no coin flip , naive regularized ML suffers from regularization bias ; Double/Debiased ML uses cross-fitting and residual-on-residual regression Neyman orthogonality to recover valid causal effects MATH . - Core questions: When is a covariate safe to adjust for pre-treatment vs. post-treatment ? How do we use tree/neural models for causal inference without regularization bias? - Real-world reach: Experimentation platforms Microsoft/Netflix/Airbnb , pricing elasticity, and marketplace policy evaluation EconML . --- From a line to a GLM OLS assumes MATH with MATH . A Generalized Linear Model McCullagh & Nelder, 1989 keeps MATH and swaps in a link MATH plus an exponential-family variance function. Logistic regression Bernoulli + logit , Poisson log-linear models for counts, and Tweedie models for zero-heavy claims are all the same unified object. Industry still fits GLMs at scale—often paired beside a neural net as Wide & Deep Cheng et al., 2016 —because GLMs are calibrated, fast, and auditable when regulators or actuaries ask for coefficient tables. python import numpy as np from scipy.optimize import minimize def poisson glm mle X, y : """ MLE for a Poisson log-link GLM without an offset. Args: X: n, p design, include a column of ones if you want an intercept y: non-negative counts Returns: beta hat """ def nll beta : eta = X @ beta y eta - exp eta is the Poisson log-likelihood up to a constant return np.mean np.exp eta - y eta start = np.zeros X.shape 1 out = minimize nll, start, method="L-BFGS-B" return out.x Mixed models when users are not i.i.d. A/B logs and longitudinal data violate independence: the same user contributes many sessions. A linear mixed model writes MATH giving each user MATH a random baseline MATH implemented in lme4 by Bates et al., 2015; see also Yu et al., 2022 . Practical rule: if treatment is assigned per user, either aggregate to one row per user or fit a mixed model with a user random intercept. Running raw OLS on event-level rows understates standard errors and creates false wins. Regression adjustment and CUPED Randomization already identifies the average treatment effect ATE . Regression here serves purely to reduce variance . Deng, Xu, Kohavi, and Walker 2013 introduced CUPED Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data : replace MATH by MATH where MATH is a pre-experiment covariate such as last week’s spend . Because MATH is independent of randomized treatment MATH , MATH is completely unbiased, while variance shrinks by MATH Lin 2013 and Reluga, Ye, and Zhao 2022 further showed that including treatment-by-covariate interactions with sandwich standard errors asymptotically guarantees variance is never worse than raw difference-in-means, and Deng et al. 2023 extended CUPED to ratio metrics and ML-predicted baselines CUPAC . --- Worked Example 1: CUPED Variance Reduction & Sample-Size Savings by Hand Suppose your weekly user spend MATH has variance MATH , and last week’s pre-experiment spend MATH correlates with MATH at MATH with MATH , so MATH : 1. Optimal CUPED coefficient: MATH . 2. Adjusted variance: MATH 3. Practical impact on experiment speed: Because required sample size scales linearly with variance MATH , cutting variance by 49% cuts required users—and experiment wait time—nearly in half ! If MATH , variance drops by MATH nearly MATH faster experiments without changing a single line of randomization! --- python import numpy as np def cuped ate y, t, x : """ Difference-in-means on a CUPED-adjusted outcome. Args: y: outcome t: 0/1 treatment x: pre-experiment covariate same length Returns: ate raw, ate cuped, theta, var reduction """ theta = np.cov y, x, ddof=1 0, 1 / np.var x, ddof=1 y cv = y - theta x - x.mean ate raw = y t == 1 .mean - y t == 0 .mean ate cv = y cv t == 1 .mean - y cv t == 0 .mean reduction = 1 - np.var y cv, ddof=1 / np.var y, ddof=1 return ate raw, ate cv, theta, reduction Centering MATH keeps the intercept readable without changing the ATE. Form the two residualized variables: MATH 3. Regress MATH on MATH : MATH . --- Worked Example 2: Partialing Out a Confounder Frisch–Waugh / DML by Hand Suppose true causal effect is MATH , but a confounder MATH e.g., “high-income user” raises both treatment probability and baseline spending: MATH . You observe 4 users: | User | Confounder MATH | Treatment MATH | Outcome MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | |------|------------------|-----------------|---------------|--------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|------------------------------------------------| | 1 | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | | 2 | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | | 3 | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | | 4 | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | MATH | Now compute the residual-on-residual slope: MATH Subtracting MATH from both MATH and MATH cleanly strips out the MATH confounder! In high dimensions, Neyman orthogonality ensures that small estimation errors in MATH and MATH multiply together MATH , vanishing fast enough for valid confidence intervals! --- python import numpy as np from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor from sklearn.model selection import KFold def dml ate y, t, X, n splits=5, random state=0 : """ Cross-fit partial-linear DML for a scalar ATE. """ y, t = np.asarray y, float , np.asarray t, float n = len y y res = np.zeros n t res = np.zeros n folds = KFold n splits=n splits, shuffle=True, random state=random state for train, test in folds.split X : my = GradientBoostingRegressor random state=random state mt = GradientBoostingRegressor random state=random state my.fit X train , y train mt.fit X train , t train y res test = y test - my.predict X test t res test = t test - mt.predict X test tau = np.dot t res, y res / np.dot t res, t res return tau Athey and Imbens 2019 and Wager and Athey 2018 Causal Forests extend the same residualization philosophy to heterogeneous treatment effects MATH . --- Explanation: Why Double ML Needs BOTH Residualization AND Cross-Fitting Why couldn’t you just run Gradient Boosting for MATH and read off the treatment effect? Walk through these four steps slowly. Step 1: Naive ML shrinkage steals credit from treatment MATH Suppose MATH is correlated with MATH . A regularized ML model shrinks MATH ’s effect slightly toward zero to reduce variance—so the leftover confounding from MATH spills directly into MATH , creating a bias of order MATH that ruins confidence intervals! Step 2: Residualizing BOTH MATH and MATH creates Neyman orthogonality By regressing MATH on MATH , first-order errors in MATH and MATH cancel out! Only their product remains: if each ML model converges at rate MATH , their product converges at MATH —restoring exact asymptotic normality. Step 3: Why cross-fitting is mandatory If you compute MATH and MATH on the same data used to train the Gradient Boosting trees, overfitting correlates the residuals and re-introduces bias! Training on Fold A and computing residuals on Fold B cross-fitting breaks that correlation completely. Step 4: Remember the one assumption ML can never fix Double ML eliminates functional-form and regularization bias—it cannot fix an unmeasured confounder missing from MATH ! No algorithm replaces domain knowledge or true randomization. --- What to use when | Setting | Tool | Why | |---|---|---| | Randomized experiment, Gaussian metric | Difference in means or CUPED / Lin | Identified by design; regression only cuts variance | | Randomized experiment, counts or binaries | GLM or transformation, then CUPED on residual | Match likelihood to outcome scale | | Repeated measures / nested users | Aggregate to assignment unit, or GLMM | Independence is false at the event level | | Observational treatment, many covariates | Double ML or a causal forest | Removes regularization bias via orthogonality | Challenges and extensions CUPED with a post -treatment covariate can subtract part of the effect; the 2013 paper is explicit that MATH must be pre-experiment. Mixed models with a small number of clusters give anti-conservative standard errors. Double ML assumes no unmeasured confounding, which no library can test away. GLMs are miscalibrated under omitted interactions; a Tweedie model that ignores a seasonal offset will look precise and be wrong. Extensions include targeted learning, policy learning from logged bandits, and the combination of CUPED with sequential tests from Chapter 06. title: 08-03-00 Optional: Modern ANOVA in Product Experiments
content: A growth team designs four new checkout buttons—Control, Green, Large, and Express—and runs all MATH pairwise MATH -tests at MATH p = 0.03 MATH , so they celebrate and ship it—unaware that under a completely true null hypothesis, six unadjusted comparisons carry roughly a 26% false-alarm rate ! Meanwhile, down the hall, another team launches a new ranking model and a new snippet UI in two separate A/B tests—completely missing the fact that the new ranking model only lifts clicks when paired with the new snippet layout! This optional lesson takes classical Chapter 08 one-way ANOVA , two-way factorial layouts , and Tukey’s HSD directly into modern multi-variant product experiments, showing how the classical variance decomposition MATH evolves naturally into variance-component mixed models when users or queries are clustered Gelman, 2005; Yu et al., 2022 . --- Key ideas: How ANOVA Powers Multi-Variant Experimentation Three classical ideas from experimental design anchor modern A/B/n and factorial platforms. 1. Omnibus Variance Decomposition One-Way ANOVA & MATH -Test Instead of spraying unadjusted pairwise MATH -tests across MATH variants, one-way ANOVA compares between-group signal MATH against within-group noise MATH via a single omnibus MATH -ratio—acting as a clean statistical gate before post-hoc pairwise inspection Tukey HSD or Benjamini–Hochberg FDR . - Core questions: Do the MATH variants differ more than random sampling noise predicts? Which post-hoc rule fits a small pre-registered family versus 50 exploratory slices? - Real-world reach: A/B/n landing-page tests, multi-arm pricing tests, and clinical dose-response comparisons. 2. Factorial Designs & Interaction Effects Two-Way ANOVA When two product changes launch together Factor A × Factor B , testing them in a single 2×2 factorial layout reuses 100% of your traffic for both main effects while explicitly measuring the interaction term MATH —revealing synergy or conflict that separate A/B tests are mathematically blind to. - Core questions: Does Feature A help only when Feature B is turned on? How do Type II vs. Type III sums of squares handle unbalanced cells? - Real-world reach: Search ranking + UI snippet co-launches, industrial design of experiments DoE , and combination drug therapies. 3. Hierarchical ANOVA & Variance Components Mixed Models Following Andrew Gelman 2005 , every row of an ANOVA table can be viewed as a variance component MATH . When each user contributes dozens of repeated sessions, moving from plain f oneway to a random-intercept mixed model fixes the denominator so clustered noise is never mistaken for treatment signal. - Core questions: How much variation comes from user-to-user differences versus within-user randomness? - Real-world reach: Repeated-measures UX studies, longitudinal app telemetry, and multi-market geo experiments. --- A/B/n is one-way ANOVA in a product coat A platform testing MATH checkout buttons is fitting the one-way layout MATH testing MATH via the omnibus MATH -statistic MATH Pairwise MATH -tests without family correction inflate Type I error across all MATH pairs. In industrial practice, assignment happens at the user level —analyzing raw session events as if they were i.i.d. rows understates MATH and manufactures fake significance. --- Worked Example 1: Computing a Complete One-Way ANOVA MATH -Test by Hand Suppose three checkout variants each have MATH users with order values $ : - Variant A: MATH mean MATH - Variant B: MATH mean MATH - Variant C: MATH mean MATH Grand mean across all MATH users: MATH . Compute every row of the ANOVA table directly: 1. Between-group Sum of Squares MATH : MATH 2. Within-group Sum of Squares MATH : Each group has sum of squared deviations MATH , so MATH 3. Omnibus MATH -statistic: MATH Verify the decomposition: MATH . Because between-group variance MATH is 12× larger than within-group noise MATH , the omnibus gate passes decisively—now you may safely run Tukey’s HSD to see which specific pairs differ! --- python import numpy as np from scipy import stats def oneway anova groups : """ Classical one-way ANOVA for a list of 1-d arrays. Returns: F, p value, ss between, ss within """ all y = np.concatenate groups grand = all y.mean ss b = sum len g g.mean - grand 2 for g in groups ss w = sum g - g.mean 2 .sum for g in groups df b = len groups - 1 df w = len all y - len groups F = ss b / df b / ss w / df w p = stats.f.sf F, df b, df w return F, p, ss b, ss w Tukey’s HSD remains the default post-hoc when every pair is interesting in a balanced design; when exploring twenty ad-hoc segments after seeing the data, switch to Chapter 06 Benjamini–Hochberg FDR . Factorial launches are two-way ANOVA Product teams rarely change one factor at a time. Crossing a new ranking model Old / New with a new snippet layout Control / Variant yields the two-way layout MATH The interaction term MATH captures whether two features amplify or cancel each other. Running two isolated A/B tests hides that interaction completely and wastes half your traffic. --- Worked Example 2: Spotting a Pure Interaction in a 2×2 Factorial Launch Suppose average user clicks in a 2×2 launch Model × Layout have the following cell means: | Ranking Model | Old Layout | New Layout | Row Mean | |---------------|------------|------------|----------| | Old Model | MATH | MATH | MATH | | New Model | MATH | MATH | MATH | | Column Mean | MATH | MATH | Grand Mean MATH | Look what happens if you run two separate one-factor A/B tests: - Test New Model only on Old Layout: MATH vs. MATH → 0 lift! Team kills the New Model! - Test New Layout only on Old Model: MATH vs. MATH → 0 lift! Team kills the New Layout! Both isolated A/B tests fail completely—yet inside a 2×2 factorial ANOVA , the interaction contrast MATH clicks lights up immediately, revealing that the New Model and New Layout unlock +80% lift together! --- python import statsmodels.api as sm from statsmodels.formula.api import ols def two way anova table df : """ Two-way ANOVA with interaction via OLS. df columns: y float , model A/B , layout A/B """ fit = ols "y ~ C model C layout ", data=df .fit return sm.stats.anova lm fit, typ=2 Type II versus Type III sums of squares matter once cells are unbalanced—pre-register your choice rather than shopping after seeing MATH -values. From the ANOVA table to mixed models Gelman 2005 reframed ANOVA as a hierarchical variance-component model : MATH where batch MATH users, queries, markets, days is a random effect with variance MATH . As Yu et al. 2022 emphasize, running plain ANOVA on repeated observations from the same user ignores clustering. Follow three crisp rules: 1. One aggregated metric per assigned user → classical one-way/two-way ANOVA or OLS is valid. 2. Multiple repeated sessions per user → fit a mixed model with a user random intercept. 3. Read the variance components MATH vs. MATH to understand how much noise is user-level vs. session-level. python import numpy as np import statsmodels.formula.api as smf def mixed treatment test df : """ Random intercept for user; fixed treatment. df columns: y, treatment, user """ model = smf.mixedlm "y ~ treatment", df, groups=df "user" return model.fit --- Explanation: Why ANOVA, Regression, and Mixed Models Are One Unified Machine Students often learn MATH -tests, ANOVA, linear regression, and mixed models in separate chapters as if they were unrelated recipes. Walk through these four steps to see that they are all the exact same linear model. Step 1: One-way ANOVA IS linear regression with dummy indicators Coding MATH variants with MATH binary indicators MATH turns MATH into ordinary OLS! The overall regression MATH -test is numerically identical to f oneway . Step 2: Two-way ANOVA simply adds product interaction columns Adding MATH creates one extra product column whose regression coefficient tests whether the two features combine additively or synergistically. Step 3: Why clustering breaks the classical MATH denominator Classical ANOVA divides by MATH assuming all MATH rows are independent. If 100 users each contribute 50 sessions MATH , treating those 5,000 rows as independent fools the MATH -test into thinking you have MATH more independent units than you actually do! Step 4: Mixed models repair the denominator by splitting variance into two layers Adding MATH separates within-user noise MATH from between-user noise MATH , restoring honest degrees of freedom and valid MATH -values on the treatment effect. --- Post-hoc choices that match the decision | Decision after a significant omnibus | Tool | Why | |---|---|---| | Which of a few pre-registered variants wins? | Tukey HSD or a single planned contrast | Family is small and closed | | Which of many slices moved? | Benjamini–Hochberg Chapter 06 | Family is large and exploratory | | Did anything move at all, for a ship/no-ship gate? | Omnibus MATH or a pre-registered OEC | Avoids pairwise fishing | | Are users or queries a source of noise? | Mixed model / variance components | Classical MATH is wrong | A common 2022–2026 pattern on experimentation platforms is: omnibus test on the overall evaluation criterion, Tukey or a pre-registered contrast on the variants, and FDR on the fifty diagnostic metrics that nobody pre-registered. Mixing those three jobs into one unadjusted table is how A/B/n acquires a reputation for false wins. Challenges and extensions ANOVA assumes constant variance and, in the classical derivation, Gaussian errors. Conversion rates near 0 or 1, and revenue with a point mass at zero, violate both; a GLM or a transformation is then the Chapter 07 companion, not a reason to abandon the decomposition. Unbalanced cells, missing variants, and sequential peeking Chapter 06 all change the finite-sample Type I error of the MATH -test. Mixed models with few groups estimate MATH badly; aggregating may be safer. Extensions include permutation ANOVA when the Gaussian assumption is implausible, aligned-rank transforms in human-computer interaction studies, and Bayesian hierarchical ANOVA when many weak factors share a prior—the setting Gelman originally had in mind.
